title: A theory of multilevel interactive equilibrium in neuroAI.
journal: Neural networks : the official journal of the International Neural Network Society
abstract: We propose a class of game-theoretic framework for adaptive multi-agent intelligent systems. Unlike the classical game theory which assumes that strategies are primitive objects chosen by perfectly rational agents, the new framework provides a mathematical foundation for studying equilibrium in NeuroAI and can be viewed as an extension of game theory with relaxed assumptions such as various degrees of uncertainty. At its core, Multilevel Interactive Equilibrium (MIE) generalizes the classical Nash equilibrium to intelligent systems with internal computation. Rather than being defined solely at the level of observable behavior, equilibrium emerges when neural learning dynamics, cognitive representations, and behavioral strategies mutually stabilize between interacting agents. This framework applies uniformly to interactions between two biological brains, two artificial agents, or hybrid human-AI systems. We discuss the emerging applications of multilevel game theory for human-autonomous vehicle driving, human-machine interactions, human-large language model (LLM) interactions, and computational psychiatry. We use simple computer simulations to provide proof-of-concept validation of MIE. We also outline experimental strategies and computational methods to estimate MIE and discuss challenges and prospects in future research.

title: Functional neurological disorder and migraine: a cross-sectional health-related quality of life study.
abstract: Functional neurological disorder (FND) and migraine are common disorders accounting for substantial health-related quality of life (HRQoL) impairment, yet comparative data are sparse. We performed a single-centre cross-sectional study of adult patients with a diagnosis of FND or migraine followed in a tertiary neurology outpatient clinic. Patients with both conditions were excluded. Data were collected through an online questionnaire and hospital records. Variables included age, sex, timing of diagnosis and treatment, comorbid pain-related and psychiatric disorders, psychological distress assessed through Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale, and Patient Global Impression of Change (PGIC) after treatment. The primary outcome measure-HRQoL-was assessed using the SF-36. Multivariable linear regression models explored the independent association between diagnosis (FND vs migraine) and HRQoL. Sixty-eight patients were included (27 with FND; 41 patients with migraine; mean age 31.1 years). Unadjusted analyses showed significantly lower HRQoL in FND across all SF-36 domains, with clinically meaningful effect sizes. FND was associated with greater psychological distress and lower perceived improvement. After adjustment for psychological distress and pain-related comorbidities, FND was still associated with worse scores in the physical functioning, physical role limitations, and social functioning domains of the SF-36. This study highlights that impairments in physical and social functioning are independent from psychiatric comorbidities in FND probably reflecting disease-specific mechanisms and a widespread impact of this condition. Yet, transdiagnostic factors-particularly psychological distress and comorbid chronic pain largely account for HRQoL impairment in both FND and migraine, with relevance for multidisciplinary treatment approaches.

title: Inertial measurement unit-based gait analysis for objective assessment of vestibular rehabilitation.
abstract: Acute vestibular syndrome (AVS), defined by sudden onset of dizziness, nausea, impaired balance and gait instability, severely affects normal daily activities. Vestibular rehabilitation alleviates the condition and facilitates the return to normal activities. This study assessed the rehabilitation process of 30 participants with AVS using Inertial Measurement Unit (IMU)-based gait analysis during timed 25-ft walk tests (T25FW) conducted at onset, after a 6-week rehabilitation program, and at a 12-week follow-up. 54 healthy controls also performed the T25FW on one occasion. Gait variables based on either five lower body sensors or only the pelvis sensor were investigated. Clinical variables: walking speed and Vertigo Symptom Scale-Short Form (VSS-SF) vertigo-balance subscale (VSS-V) were also recorded. Significant successive improvements in VSS-V were observed between all timepoints. Furthermore, walking speed, Gait Profile Score (GPS), pelvis GPS, and cadence decreased from onset to the end of the rehabilitation period, after which changes were not significant. Walking speed was slower for the AVS group at baseline (0.65 m/s, p < 0.0001) and at 12 weeks (1.13 m/s, p < 0.05) compared to controls (1.26 m/s). GPS, pelvis GPS, GPS asymmetry, and cadence were significantly greater compared to controls at baseline (6.8° vs. 4.4°, 3.6° vs. 2.6°, and 87 steps/min vs. 118 steps/min, respectively, p < 0.0001). GPS asymmetry was also higher at baseline compared to controls (1.40 steps/min vs. 0.80 steps/min, p < 0.05). In conclusion, gait improvement was captured via IMU-based gait analysis, even when using a single sensor, supporting the clinical feasibility of using both single- and multi-sensor wearable systems for rehabilitation assessment.

title: Prevalence and outcomes of co-occurring mental/physical comorbidities and substance use disorders: An atlas umbrella review including 156 systematic reviews with meta-analysis.
journal: European neuropsychopharmacology : the journal of the European College of Neuropsychopharmacology
abstract: Substance use disorders(SUDs) are intertwined with psychiatric and general medical disorders. Substances of abuse also exert intrinsic toxicities and adverse effects that contribute to extensive somatic multimorbidity, complicating patient prognoses. This umbrella review(UR) systematically aggregated, harmonized, and graded the credibility of meta-analytic evidence concerning SUD comorbidities across psychiatric/somatic dimensions. We searched major electronic databases up to July 2026 for systematic reviews with meta-analyses of observational studies mapping SUD co-occurrences. Extracted data were categorized by ICD-11 diagnostic blocks. Meta-analytic estimates were evaluated using pre-registered quantitative credibility indicators assessing sample size(N), number of studies(k), 95%confidence interval(95%CI) widths, and heterogeneity(I2). The review included 156 systematic reviews with meta-analysis, encompassing 100,441,167 database/registry records across 14,322 study entries, with possible overlap across reviews. High-credibility data showed a strong intra-block psychiatric overlap: Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder demonstrated a pooled SUD prevalence of 21.0%(95%CI=17.0-25.0%;k = 31), while Major Depressive Disorder reached a prevalence of 36.1%(95%CI=32.4%-39.7%;k = 161) among patients with Opioid Use Disorder(OUD). Somatic toxicities and iatrogenic pathways were highly prevalent: opioid analgesic use in chronic noncancer pain 27.0%(95%C.I.=23.0-31.0%;N > 3.9 M), and in post-lumbar fusion surgery patients (40.0%;95%C.I.=32.0-49.0%). High prevalences of syndemic infectious comorbidities were observed among populations with injection drug use, with Hepatitis C virus prevalence reaching 61.0%(95%CI=56.0-67.0%) in regional cohorts. Highly specific associations revealed that schizotypal traits strongly correlate with Cannabis Use Disorder(I2=0%). SUDs are multi-systemic disorders characterized by substantial cross-block psychiatric/medical multimorbidity. The breadth and the credibility gradient of multimorbidity argue for routine cross-domain screening and coordinated care, with model effectiveness left to trials.

title: Electrical stimulation targeting optic nerve regeneration following acute and chronic neuropathies.
abstract: Optic neuropathies such as glaucoma or optic neuritis are conditions whereby the optic nerve is damaged by mechanisms including ischemia, compression, inflammation or immune-mediated processes, leading to progressive degeneration of retinal ganglion cells and subsequent loss of vision. Strategies including medication and surgery help to slow down these diseases but fail to repair the neurons of the optic nerve themselves. In this review, we first detail the range of optic nerve neuropathies and their current front line treatment options, briefly outline various experimental treatment strategies and their limitations, before focusing on electrical stimulation as a treatment strategy, covering the current state of the art and potential routes for further development.

title: Effectiveness of mindfulness-based interventions in UHR individuals and patients experiencing a first episode of psychosis: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
abstract: Guided and structured mindfulness-based interventions (MBIs) have shown good tolerance and promising effects on negative effects and psychosocial functioning. The evaluation of these approaches in Ultra High Risk (UHR) populations or during first-episode psychosis (FEP) is developing. This systematic review and meta-analysis aims to examine the effectiveness of MBIs in these populations. A systematic search was conducted (PubMed, PsychInfo, Embase, ClinicalTrials.gov). The included studies offered MBIs to participants meeting UHR and FEP criteria. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) were included in a meta-analysis using a random-effects model. Three RCTs, three prospective studies, one qualitative study, and one case study published between 2013 and 2023 were selected. The studies suggest perceived benefits for stress management, self-reassurance and feelings of empowerment. The meta-analysis, based on only two RCTs comparing MBIs with treatment as usual, shows a significant post-intervention effect on negative symptoms (SMD = -0.67 [-1.12, -0.22]), which was not maintained at the 3-month follow-up (SMD = -0.40 [-0.99, 0.19]). Furthermore, no significant effect of MBIs on quality of life, social functioning, or mindfulness ability was observed, either immediately after the intervention or at the 3-month follow-up. MBIs appear promising in UHR and FEP but evidence remains limited with small RCT pool, limited durability at follow-up, heterogeneity of patients and MBIs studied . Well-designed RCTs using standardized mindfulness protocols and relevant outcome measures are needed to confirm their usefulness in early intervention.

title: Emerging strategies for progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP) combination therapies.
abstract: Progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP) is a neurodegenerative disorder characterised by a combination of motor, ocular, cognitive, and behavioural impairment, but has a heterogeneous clinical presentation. It is a devastating and rapidly progressive atypical parkinsonian disorder with no current disease-modifying treatments. PSP is classified as a primary tauopathy characterised by abnormal accumulation of tau within neurons and glial cells, primarily in the brain stem, culminating in cell death. While genome wide association studies have been instrumental in identifying multiple risk loci, recent multi-omics studies combining brain gene expression and other omics measures have revealed a plethora of perturbed transcripts and molecular pathways that may play pivotal roles in PSP. This includes genes such as MAPT, STOM, KANK2, DDR2, LRRK2, and STX6, but their precise roles remain elusive. These genes are differentially expressed and may regulate processes including neuroinflammation, glymphatic clearance of tau, cytoskeletal maintenance, and synaptic function. In this review, we summarise current treatment strategies attempted in PSP, compile disease-modifying therapies in development, and explore potential disease mechanisms suggested by multi-omics studies. By targeting several underlying disease processes at once, combination strategies have the potential to improve both motor and cognitive function, slow neurodegeneration, and ultimately alter disease progression.

title: GPU-accelerated spherical-deconvolution informed filtering of tractograms for quantitative diffusion MRI connectomics.
abstract: Streamline tractography from diffusion magnetic resonance imaging is the standard technique for mapping the structural connections of the human brain, but raw tractograms contain systematic streamline-density biases that undermine quantitative connectivity analysis. Spherical-deconvolution informed filtering of tractograms (SIFT) and its successor SIFT2 correct these biases by matching streamline densities to the underlying fibre orientation distributions; however, their computational cost-from tens of minutes to several hours for a 10-million-streamline tractogram-restricts their use in large cohort studies. We describe the design, implementation and validation of graphics processing unit (GPU) implementations of both algorithms using the CUDA programming model. A two-stage architecture retains the reference CPU implementation for streamline-to-fixel mapping and offloads only the optimisation phase to the GPU, so that the accelerated code can be validated directly against the reference software on identical inputs. On tractograms of 10 million streamlines from four subjects drawn from the UK Biobank and the Human Connectome Project, the GPU SIFT implementation ran 25 to 56 times faster than the multi-threaded CPU reference while selecting an essentially identical streamline subset (at most 30 of 10 6 retained streamlines differed per subject; overlap at least 99.997%). The GPU SIFT2 implementation ran 6.8 to 9.3 times faster with a coefficient of determination of at least 0.999998 between GPU and CPU streamline weights. Both implementations accept unmodified MRtrix3 inputs and produce outputs in the same formats as the reference commands, allowing direct substitution into existing tractography pipelines.

title: Isavuconazole in the management of central nervous system fungal infections: Parenchymal penetration and clinical performance.
abstract: Invasive fungal infections (IFIs) involving the central nervous system (CNS) represent a critical challenge, with mortality of 50% or more in cerebral aspergillosis, mucormycosis, fusariosis and cryptococcal meningitis, and pharmacokinetic (PK) access restricted by the blood-brain barrier (BBB). This review analyzes the clinical performance and parenchymal penetration of isavuconazole (ISA), a second-generation triazole. ISA exhibits linear PK, a cyclodextrin-free intravenous formulation, and high tissue affinity, favored by moderate lipophilicity (experimental logP 2.56) and in vitro inhibition of P-glycoprotein and breast cancer resistance protein (BCRP) efflux transporters. Experimental evidence from animal models shows brain-to-plasma ratios of 0.42 to 1.8, indicating efficient BBB crossing. Human biopsy data show a fundamental PK dichotomy. While cerebrospinal fluid concentrations are restricted (about 1% of plasma), levels in fungal abscesses and inflamed parenchyma reach up to 5.11 mg/L, exceeding the minimum inhibitory concentration reported for Aspergillus fumigatus in those cases. Clinically, ISA was associated with a response in 70% of first-line (n = 10) and 73% of salvage-treated patients (n = 30) with cerebral aspergillosis, and 82% of 28 patients with CNS-only coccidioidomycosis improved or stabilized. Meta-analyses suggest fewer drug-related adverse events and, in randomized subgroups, fewer hepatobiliary events compared with voriconazole, although moderate cytochrome P450 3A4 inhibition warrants monitoring of calcineurin and mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) inhibitors in transplant recipients. ISA is a strategic option for high-complexity CNS-involving IFIs, serving as a therapeutic alternative in salvage and prolonged-maintenance settings, though first-line use in CNS infection awaits confirmation from randomized trials.

title: From Exposure to Disease: Prevalence of Post-Mononucleosis Multiple Sclerosis.
Association of Prethrombectomy Hemorrhagic Infarction on MRI With Further Transformation and Functional Outcomes: A Multicenter Study.
abstract: Mechanical thrombectomy (MT) is the standard of care for acute ischemic stroke from large vessel occlusion (LVO). Although postprocedural parenchymal hematoma (PH) predicts poor outcomes, pretreatment hemorrhagic infarction (HI), defined as petechial bleeding within infarcted tissue, is traditionally viewed as a benign radiologic finding. Its significance on sensitive preintervention MRI remains underexplored. We evaluated whether pretreatment MRI HI is associated with 90-day functional dependence, post-MT PH, and symptomatic intracerebral hemorrhage (SICH). This retrospective cohort study included consecutive patients with anterior circulation LVO undergoing MT at 2 stroke centers (2015-2022). Patients required pre-MT T2*-weighted MRI. HI was graded (types I/II) per European Cooperative Acute Stroke Study III criteria in blinded fashion. The primary outcome was 90-day functional dependence (modified Rankin Scale 3-6). Secondary outcomes were post-MT ipsilateral PH and SICH. We used multivariable Bayesian and frequentist logistic regression to adjust for age, sex, NIH Stroke Scale, baseline disability, comorbidities, infarct volume, and procedural factors. Among 479 patients (median age 72 years; 46% female; 50% received IV thrombolysis), pretreatment HI was identified in 25 (5.2%), with excellent inter-rater agreement (Cohen κ = 0.9). Functional dependence at 90 days occurred in 47% of the total cohort, ipsilateral PH in 9.4%, and SICH in 3.1%. In multivariable analysis, pre-MT HI was independently associated with 90-day functional dependence (Bayesian adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 6.66, 95% credible interval [CrI] 2.15-24.28, Pr[OR > 1] = 1.00; frequentist aOR 5.95, 95% CI 1.91-18.52, p = 0.002). Pre-MT HI also demonstrated a high posterior probability of association with post-MT ipsilateral PH (Bayesian aOR 2.76, 95% CrI 0.73-9.26, Pr[OR > 1] = 0.94; frequentist aOR 2.84, 95% CI 0.84-9.58, p = 0.091) and SICH (Bayesian aOR 5.59, 95% CrI 0.63-34.92, Pr[OR > 1] = 0.95; frequentist aOR 6.02, 95% CI 1.00-36.11, p = 0.049). HI detected on pretreatment MRI is an independent predictor of poor long-term functional outcomes and correlates with post-MT PH/SICH. Pre-MT HI may reflect significant blood-brain barrier disruption and microvascular fragility, serving as a marker of reperfusion vulnerability. Limitations include the retrospective design and the relatively low frequency of HI, PH, and SICH, which were addressed using Bayesian modeling to quantify uncertainty. Although not a contraindication to MT, identifying HI may aid in periprocedural risk stratification and serve as a candidate marker for future neuroprotective trials.

title: Increased Need for High Levels of Care in Patients with Delirium Superimposed on Dementia and Risk of Malnutrition.
journal: Journal of nutrition in gerontology and geriatrics
abstract: We examined the impact of a malnutrition risk (Malnutrition Universal Screening Tool (MUST) score ≥1) in patients with delirium superimposed on dementia (DSD) on the need for higher levels of care on discharge. The associations of risk categories (defined as: i, well-nourished patients with delirium but without dementia and; ii, DSD or malnutrition risk; and iii, DSD & malnutrition risk) with care needs were evaluated by multivariable logistic regression. These were expressed as odds ratios (OR) and 95% confidence intervals (95% CI), adjusted for age, sex, polypharmacy and anticholinergic burden. In total, 554 consecutive patients admitted to a single UK secondary hospital, aged 61.3-105.3 years (mean = 85.5 ± 7.6 years), were enrolled for whom: 75.1% were from their own home; 36.3% exhibited underlying DSD; and 47.5% had malnutrition at admission. Compared to well-nourished patients with delirium but without dementia, those with both DSD and a malnutrition risk had greater needs for new care-home placement [OR = 2.75, 95%CI 1.46-5.20], and a discharge delay due to waiting for a package of care, a suitable placement, or equipment [OR = 2.54, 95%CI 1.46-4.41], and were proportionally less functionally independent. Malnutrition risk amongst patients with DSD who were admitted to hospital increased the need for higher levels of care at discharge. Prevention of malnutrition for patients with underlying dementia is essential to reduce hospitalization and improve care needs.

title: Predictors of Discordance Between Neurological and Quality-of-Life Recovery After Surgery for Degenerative Cervical Myelopathy: A Retrospective Cohort Study.
abstract: Retrospective analysis of prospectively collected multicentre cohort data. Quantify discordance between neurological recovery (modified Japanese Orthopaedic Association [mJOA]) and quality-of-life (QoL) recovery (SF-36 PCS) after surgery for degenerative cervical myelopathy (DCM) and identify predictors of each profile. Neurological and patient-reported outcomes capture different dimensions of recovery after DCM surgery, but the frequency, structure, and baseline correlates of discordance between these outcome domains remain incompletely characterized. Retrospective analysis of prospective multicentre AO Spine CSM-NA and CSM-I cohorts. Recovery used published minimum clinically important differences (MCID) for mJOA and SF-36 PCS at 12 months, with 6-month values carried forward when unavailable. Patients were classified as concordant recovery, neurological-only recovery, QoL-only recovery, or no recovery. Discordant recovery was defined as achieving one MCID without the other. Baseline predictors were estimated by multinomial logistic regression using multiple imputation (m=20) for missing covariates. Of 353 patients, 310 were classifiable: 88 (28.4%) concordant, 50 (16.1%) neurological-only, 82 (26.5%) QoL-only, 90 (29.0%) no recovery; 132 (42.6%) discordant. Higher baseline PCS predicted neurological-only versus concordant recovery (OR 4.42 per SD, 95% CI 2.34-8.35), whereas higher baseline mJOA predicted QoL-only (OR 5.67, 2.95-10.90) and no recovery (OR 4.23, 2.25-7.95; all P <0.001). Older age, higher Nurick grade, lower mental component score and greater frailty also predicted non-concordant profiles. In exploratory models, ossification of the posterior longitudinal ligament predicted no recovery (OR 5.71, 2.17-15.0) and number of compressed levels predicted neurological-only recovery (OR 1.85, 1.17-2.92). Neurological-only patients improved less in pain-related disability (NDI Q1) than concordant or QoL-only patients (P <0.02). Neurological and QoL recovery were discordant in over 40% of patients and governed by different baseline variables. Neurological-only recovery reflects limited room for measurable QoL gain, compounded by persistent pain, rather than surgical failure. III.

title: Acute doses of 3 and 6 mg/kg caffeine produce outcome- and phase-specific improvements in male 100-m sprinters: A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial.
abstract: Evidence is limited on whether commonly used caffeine doses provide uniform benefits across sprint phases and performance outcomes in trained sprinters. We compared the acute effects of 3 and 6 mg/kg caffeine in a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, three-condition crossover trial. Twenty-one male 100-m sprinters completed placebo, 3 mg/kg caffeine, and 6 mg/kg caffeine trials separated by at least 7 days. Sixty minutes after ingestion, participants completed two maximal 60-m sprints, followed by countermovement jump, squat jump, and 10-s Wingate tests. Sprint times, derived split times, start reaction time, starting-block rate of force development, stride variables, and perceived exertion were also assessed. Linear mixed-effects models adjusting for treatment period and randomized sequence showed clear treatment effects for cumulative 10-, 30-, and 60-m times (all p < 0.001). Relative to placebo, 3 mg/kg shortened these times by 0.056, 0.083, and 0.123 s, whereas 6 mg/kg shortened them by 0.075, 0.115, and 0.175 s. Compared with 3 mg/kg, 6 mg/kg further reduced 30- and 60-m times by 0.032 and 0.052 s, respectively, whereas the additional 0.019-s reduction at 10 m was not statistically significant in the primary mixed-effects model. Both doses improved reaction time, perceived exertion, jump height, Wingate peak and mean power, and starting-block rate of force development relative to placebo. Additional benefits of 6 mg/kg were evident for jump height and rate of force development, but not for reaction time, perceived exertion, or Wingate mean power; Wingate peak power did not improve further with the higher dose. Stride length and frequency were unchanged. These findings indicate outcome-specific dose responses, with 3 mg/kg improving multiple performance outcomes and 6 mg/kg providing additional benefits most consistently for vertical jump height, starting-block rate of force development, and cumulative performance over the first 60 m. Chinese Clinical Trial Registry, ChiCTR2600128594.

title: Rethinking psychosocial rehabilitation in mental health.
abstract: Psychosocial rehabilitation is central to recovery-oriented mental health care, yet its uptake remains uneven because of persistent conceptual, methodological, organisational, and implementation barriers.Greater conceptual clarity is needed through stakeholder dialogue to establish a common set of core principles that can be adapted across diverse cultural and health system contexts.Meaningful co-creation with people with lived experience and their families should be embedded throughout the research and implementation cycle, from priority setting and intervention design to evaluation, scale-up, and dissemination.Evidence synthesis should adopt component-based and mechanism-informed approaches to identify the active components of psychosocial rehabilitation interventions and the mechanisms through which they produce change.Psychosocial rehabilitation should be recognised as a core component of mental healthcare, integrated from first contact and delivered across the continuum of care.

title: Spatial transcriptomics reveals organizational properties of the mouse spinal cord and alterations in neuropathic pain.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
abstract: The spinal cord integrates diverse somatosensory inputs and executes motor outputs through anatomically and functionally distinct circuits. Here, we employed spatially resolved single-cell transcriptomic profiling of the adult mouse spinal cord to gain insights into the organizational logic of the spinal cord. Our results reveal distinct spatial and laminar distributions of neuronal subtypes, including axial level and sex-specific differences. Many neuronal subtypes exhibit lamina-specific somatic proximities, suggesting potential regionally specific connectivity. Additionally, neuronal subtypes within the dorsal horn exhibit a wide range of predicted cell-cell communication motifs, as assessed by the spatial distribution of neuropeptide- and other ligand-receptor pairs. Finally, we identified several neuronal subtypes with altered transcriptomic states and predicted cell-cell communications in a model of neuropathic pain. This spatially resolved cellular and molecular map of the spinal cord will facilitate the decoding of circuit mechanisms underlying somatosensory and motor functions in health and disease.

title: Increased proteasome and inflammasome activity in response to cellular stress and PTSD-induced damage - a narrative review.
abstract: Aim: This review summarizes current evidence regarding increased proteasome and inflammasome activity in response to cellular stress and PTSD-induced neuronal injury. Materials and Methods: A narrative literature review was conducted using PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar databases. Studies published between 2015 and 2025 were analyzed using keywords including "PTSD," "proteasome," "inflammasome," "NLRP3," "oxidative stress," and "neuroinflammation." Experimental and clinical studies investigating molecular mechanisms associated with PTSD-related cellular stress were included. The reviewed studies demonstrated that chronic traumatic stress promotes excessive activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome and dysregulation of proteasome activity. These changes contribute to accumulation of damaged proteins, mitochondrial impairment, increased reactive oxygen species production, and elevated secretion of pro-inflammatory cytokines, including interleukin-1β and interleukin-18. Persistent activation of these pathways is associated with microglial activation, synaptic dysfunction, impaired neuroplasticity, and progressive neuronal degeneration in PTSD. Conclusions: Proteasome and inflammasome dysregulation play an important role in the neurobiology of PTSD and may contribute to chronic neuroinflammatory and neurodegenerative processes. Targeting these pathways may represent a promising therapeutic strategy for reducing neuronal damage associated with traumatic stress.

title: Adrenal hormone and histamine levels in children with vasomotor rhinitis.
abstract: Aim: To study the levels of adrenal hormones and histamine in children with vasomotor rhinitis. Materials and Methods: Hormones secreted by the adrenal glands are active biological regulators of metabolism in the body. Research into the hormonal function of the adrenal glands is of great importance for studying the pathogenesis of certain allergic diseases. Spectrofluorometric blood examination for the presence of 11-OCS (sum total content of hydrocortisone and corticosterone) and histamine, and also examina￢tion of the urine for adrenaline and noradrenaline content were conducted in children suffering from vasomotor rhinitis. Results: The results obtained were statistically proces￢ses and considered from the aspect of dependence on the form of vasomotor rhinitis (allergic and nonallergic rhinitis) and age. Apparently healthy children (30) were examined biochemically for control. An increased content of the adrenal gland hor￢mones (11-OCS) was found to be present in the blood of children with vasomotor rhinitis. Histamine content was elevated only in children with an allergic rhinitis. Adrenaline and noradrenaline excretion increased with the advance of age, but was unchanged in rhinitis. Conclusions: Consequently, in this disease there was a functional reaction of the adrenal cortex, but no functional changes occurred in the medulla. An increa￢sed histamine content confirmed the allergic nature of the disease.

title: Effects of Remote Ischemic Conditioning on Cerebral Blood Flow Regulation in Atherosclerosis: A Randomized Trial.
journal: Annals of the New York Academy of Sciences
abstract: Impaired dynamic cerebral autoregulation (dCA) contributes to cerebral perfusion instability in patients with cerebrovascular atherosclerosis. Remote ischemic conditioning (RIC) has shown neuroprotective potential; however, its acute effects on dCA in this population remain unclear. In this randomized, sham-controlled trial, patients with intracranial atherosclerotic stenosis (ICAS) and/or extracranial atherosclerotic stenosis (ECAS) received a single session of RIC or sham-RIC. dCA was assessed at baseline and at 0-1, 6-9, and 24 h using transfer function analysis. The prespecified primary endpoint was the affected-side phase difference (PD) at 6-9 h. Of the 140 randomized participants, 132 with valid primary endpoint data were included in the primary analysis. For the primary outcome, the affected-side PD at 6-9 h was significantly greater in the RIC group than in the sham-RIC group (adjusted β = 12.166, 95% CI: 6.787-17.545; p < 0.001). Secondary analyses at other time points and of the unaffected side supported an acute physiological effect of RIC on dCA. These findings suggest that a single RIC session may rapidly improve impaired dCA in patients with ICAS and/or ECAS. Larger studies are needed to determine whether this response varies across clinical presentations and vascular territories.

title: Protocol for the production of high-yielded research-grade AAV vectors in transiently transfected HEK293T cells.
abstract: Adeno-associated vector is a platform of choice for delivering genome-editing toolkits, due to its transient and robust expression. Here, we present a protocol for viral production for in vivo use. We describe steps for transfecting producer cells, harvesting virus, and purifying/concentrating viral particles. We then detail procedures for estimating viral titers. This protocol ensures high viral yields and transduction competency and is scalable to meet user-customized production needs. For complete details on the use of this protocol, please refer to Kantor et al.1.

title: Mouse APOE Christchurch protects against Aβ-induced tau and α-synuclein aggregation.
abstract: Apolipoprotein E (APOE) genotype alters the risk for Alzheimer's disease (AD) but also affects dementia risk in Parkinson's disease (PD) and dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB). Recent evidence suggests that the APOE Christchurch (CC) mutation protects against AD, however, its effects on PD and DLB are unknown. We generated an APOE CC knock-in mouse to understand its effects on amyloid-β (Aβ), tau, and α-synuclein (α-syn) aggregation. APOE CC mice show increased plasma cholesterol and triglyceride levels, decreased Aβ and Aβ-induced tau pathology after intracortical AD-tau injection into 5xFAD mice but do not change Aβ or tau pathology in individual transgenic mouse models without injection. Interestingly, APOE CC reduces formation and spread of α-syn aggregation in the brain, peripheral-to-spinal cord spread, and directly increases binding affinity to α-syn compared to APOE WT. Our study emphasizes the remarkable protective effects of a point mutation in murine APOE against Aβ-induced tau and α-syn aggregation.

title: The six capacities of responsible autonomy: naturalizing free will in biological and artificial systems.
journal: Philosophical transactions of the Royal Society of London. Series B, Biological sciences
abstract: The rapid integration of agentic AI is intensifying disputes about artificial autonomy, widening an agency schism between normative frameworks that presuppose agency and a scientific ontology that denies it. This paper proposes a revisionary naturalization: free will designates the control interface that embodied agents evolved to navigate social worlds pervaded by hidden intentional states, not a metaphysical ornament. The antinomy between determinism and libertarian freedom is dissolved by analysing free will from the perspective of control mechanisms. Diagnosing the philosophical record and systems neuroscience, I specify six capacities that naturalize free will as Responsible Autonomy: Active Decoupling, Endogenous Drive, Leeway, Normative Self-Governance, Diachronic Integrity and Experiential Ownership. These are proposed as control constraints on any responsible agent, and hence as design constraints for model construction and as a checklist for evaluating responsible agency in biological and artificial systems. A companion paper maps each capacity to the Distributed Adaptive Control theory of volition and agency, its neurobiological substrates and the Evaluation Suite for Responsible Autonomy (ESRA) test, supplying, in Carnap's terms, the precision and predictive power that complete the explication. This article is part of the discussion meeting issue 'From being to identity: analysis and synthesis of the self'.

title: Building a robotic self.
journal: Philosophical transactions of the Royal Society of London. Series B, Biological sciences
abstract: I wake up in the morning, I see my hand and I know it is me. This seemingly simple skill lies at the foundation of our agentive selves. We assume that the development of the self, in both biological and synthetic agents, is grounded in sensorimotor embodiment and inductive learning biases, as well as in the principle of predictive coding. Here, we explore the core inductive biases and process components for building a robotic minimal self. We propose that the formation of a hierarchical, generative model of the self is driven by active inference processes that interactively infer both an endogenous contextual frame and behaviour within this frame. Accordingly, experimental implementations in humanoid robots show how body ownership and agency can develop as foundational computational components. This work on building a robotic minimal self outlines future research directions in mechanistic modelling of the development of an artificial self. To probe the depth of this development, we sketch out embodied Turing tests that challenge complex problem-solving skills, as well as social intelligence and theory of mind. We suggest that uncertainty resolution and the social domain may be promising avenues for further research in the near future. This article is part of the discussion meeting issue 'From being to identity: analysis and synthesis of the self'.

title: Making sense of sensation: a framework of interoceptive attribution and appraisal with clinical applications.
journal: Philosophical transactions of the Royal Society of London. Series B, Biological sciences
abstract: Interoception provides a link between bodily states and cognitive and affective processes across both unconscious and conscious domains and is fundamental for a coherent sense of self. While previous research linking interoception to mental health has predominantly focused on interoceptive accuracy, attention, self-beliefs and insight, we argue that the higher-order interpretation of consciously perceived bodily signals plays a fundamental and underexplored role in this relationship. We propose a framework delineating two higher-order processes-interoceptive attribution and appraisal-which constitute the interpretation of interoceptive sensations that reach conscious awareness. We outline key factors that modulate attention, attribution and appraisal, and evidence the relevance of this framework to mental health conditions. Given that these processes are accessible to cognition, they represent an important target for existing psychotherapeutic interventions. We integrate such interventions within our framework, highlighting their potential to enhance interoception-based therapeutic approaches. This article is part of the discussion meeting issue 'From being to identity: analysis and synthesis of the self'.

title: Changes in self-related cognitive processes and depressive symptom severity following a single, moderate dose of psilocybin in depressed patients.
journal: Philosophical transactions of the Royal Society of London. Series B, Biological sciences
abstract: Psychedelic-assisted therapy, particularly with psilocybin, is increasingly proposed as a treatment for major depressive disorder, yet the neural and psychological mechanisms underlying its effects remain under investigation. In a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled clinical trial, individuals diagnosed with major depressive disorder received a single, moderate dose of psilocybin (0.215 mg kg-1) or placebo, with the same psychological support. We analysed N = 37 individuals with major depressive disorder undergoing assessments of depressive symptoms (Beck's depression inventory and Montgomery-Åsberg depression rating scale), self-concept (Frankfurt self-concept scale) and neural markers of self-referential processing using an fMRI-based task. Compared with placebo, the psilocybin group exhibited significant reductions in depressive symptoms and a significant increase in positive self-concept two weeks after substance administration. Changes in self-concept were significantly correlated with decreased depressive scores. Neuroimaging revealed psilocybin-associated modulation of caudate activation during externally oriented attention after two weeks, contrasting with placebo-induced caudate changes during self-referential processing. These findings extend prior evidence linking psychedelics to changes in self-referential processing and self-concept and demonstrate that such changes occur concurrently with reductions in depressive symptoms. Future research should aim to replicate and extend these results and refine therapy protocols targeting self-processing and self-concept in psychedelic-assisted therapy in major depressive disorder. This article is part of the discussion meeting issue 'From being to identity: analysis and synthesis of the self'.

title: The social self: integration of multimodal communication signals in dyadic interactions.
journal: Philosophical transactions of the Royal Society of London. Series B, Biological sciences
abstract: Humans are in continuous exchange with other persons, thereby integrating the individual self and the social self. This requires the production of different verbal and nonverbal signals at the subpersonal level (individual self) and, at the same time, their coordination with various perceived signals at the interpersonal level (social self). Many of our communicative signals are conveyed substantially nonverbally-that is automatically, intuitively and effortlessly, requiring dynamic coordination over time ('chronemics'). Whereas successful communication is usually perceived as pleasant and satisfying, communication can also be experienced as disrupted if chronemics do not unfold properly. With respect to the particularly informative example of autism spectrum disorder, we propose the concept of 'double invisibility'. Non-autistic persons intuitively produce and expect a rich, multimodal stream of communication signals without being aware of it (first invisibility). By contrast, autistic persons produce and expect nonverbal cues either to a significantly lesser extent or not at all without being aware of it (second invisibility). This mismatch leads to misunderstandings and disturbed communication. The coordination within the dyad that is continuously constructed through real-time communication is crucial to understand the full complexity of multimodal interactions and their disturbances. This article is part of the discussion meeting issue 'From being to identity: analysis and synthesis of the self'.

title: How does the developing mind construct a self?
journal: Philosophical transactions of the Royal Society of London. Series B, Biological sciences
abstract: Our capacity to think about ourselves is a developmental achievement that, when it emerges, profoundly changes cognition. Currently, there are few, if any mechanistic accounts of where a concept of self could come from, and empirical investigation within contemporary developmental science is surprisingly absent. Drawing on a wealth of data from cognitive neuroscience and developmental psychology, I propose a new mechanistic account of the ontogeny of our reflective self-awareness anchored in infants' interoceptive signals. This is a social cognitive account in which infants' expectations about others' attention are deeply entwined with the modulating effect that others' attention has on infants' awareness of their interoceptive state, together providing the impetus for infants to generate a conceptual representation of self de novo. This article is part of the discussion meeting issue 'From being to identity: analysis and synthesis of the self'.

title: Scaffolded acquisition of a robot self-world distinction in a layered architecture model of the developing self.
journal: Philosophical transactions of the Royal Society of London. Series B, Biological sciences
abstract: How does the sense of self emerge in human development, and could an artificial system acquire a similar sense using algorithmic principles and given a suitable embodiment and experience? Here, we describe a machine learning framework, inspired by developmental psychology and neurobiology, that acquires a self-world distinction and minimal self-model. Unlike previous approaches, we introduce a gradual formulation, integrating correlation-based and predictive techniques within a layered architecture. Using a simulated humanoid, we show first how a self-world distinction can emerge through correlation-based self-supervision. This model uses dependencies between proprioception and vision to distinguish its own body from its surroundings during infant-like motor babbling. Next, we construct a model of how these sensory signals will evolve in time. This predictive capacity uses the self-world distinction acquired by the lower layer as input to neural ordinary differential equation models that learn continuous dynamics. Finally, we demonstrate scaffolding of the higher layer by the lower one, showing that predictive learning occurs more rapidly with the lower layer already in place. By integrating these mechanisms, our approach offers a framework for characterizing a minimal robotic self that can inform our understanding of the emergence of the sense of self in the human mind/brain. This article is part of the discussion meeting issue 'From being to identity: analysis and synthesis of the self'.

title: Body in memory: the role of bodily self-consciousness in episodic memory and autonoetic consciousness.
journal: Philosophical transactions of the Royal Society of London. Series B, Biological sciences
abstract: Episodic memory (EM) enables the conscious recollection of personally experienced events, including contextual features such as visual, auditory and emotional details. However, the role of bodily signals has been largely neglected in EM, although the observer's body provides a rich bodily context during the encoding, storage and recall of events, and has recently been associated with a bodily form of self-consciousness (bodily self-consciousness; BSC). Here, we introduce key concepts and findings on BSC and then summarize recent experimental paradigms, as well as behavioural and neural evidence, on how BSC impacts EM. This includes autonoetic consciousness, a core EM feature that emphasizes the conscious re-experiencing of past events. Current evidence suggests that modulations of BSC impact later memory, including objective EM performance and subjective autonoetic recollection (and other forms of memory such as working memory). These BSC-EM effects are supported by brain mechanisms in the posterior parietal cortex (particularly the temporoparietal junction and precuneus), motor cortex (premotor cortex and supplementary motor area) and prefrontal cortex that are coupled with the hippocampal complex, mediating BSC effects in EM. Linking subjective bodily experience during encoding and retrieval to the subjective re-experiencing of past events, we highlight open questions for future research on self and memory. This article is part of the discussion meeting issue 'From being to identity: analysis and synthesis of the self'.

title: Evolutionary foundations of social identity.
journal: Philosophical transactions of the Royal Society of London. Series B, Biological sciences
abstract: Social identity theory provides a rich description of how humans relate to various kinds of social groups, but no substantive account of why human psychology evolved to be so group-minded in the first place. We propose that the evolutionarily original form of social identity was one's moral identity as a cooperative group member. For ancient humans, survival depended on being an assimilated member of a cultural group, which, in turn, competed against other groups. In this context, humans evolved skills and motivations for engaging in the collective agency of a cultural group, especially the self-reflective capacity to adopt a social identity (i.e. to construe oneself as a member of a 'we') and the concomitant self-regulatory motivation to maintain a positive social identity (i.e. to strive for 'I', the individual, to meet the standards that 'we' uphold). In this evolutionary proposal, behavioural effects of group identity, inferences of common knowledge and moral emotions are all manifestations of the function of social identity as a self-regulatory system for maintaining one's good standing as a cooperative group member. This article is part of the discussion meeting issue 'From being to identity: analysis and synthesis of the self'.

title: X-ray Crystallography of a Nanobody/JAM-1 Complex Informs Barrier Weakening and Enhanced Drug Permeability in a Cellular Blood-Brain Barrier Model.
abstract: For pharmacological treatments of brain disorders, the blood-brain barrier (BBB) poses a formidable obstacle, tightly restricting the cerebral uptake of therapeutic agents. Tight junction (TJ) binders, including peptides, proteins, and monoclonal antibodies, that specifically bind to the extracellular domains (ECDs) of TJ proteins are increasingly being explored as BBB-weakening agents for enhanced drug delivery to the brain. Given that nanobodies (Nbs) can access epitopes that are often inaccessible to conventional antibodies, we obtained 16 Nbs with unique CDRs via immunization of alpaca with the ECD of either human (h) or murine JAM-1 (mJAM-1), a major TJ protein. Twelve Nb candidates exhibited high-affinity binding to mJAM-1, as measured by surface plasmon resonance (SPR), and these interactions were further validated for 9 Nbs by immunostaining of JAM-1-overexpressing cells. Five Nbs were found to weaken the barrier of the eGFP-hCldn5-MDCKII cellular monolayer, as shown by reduced transendothelial electrical resistance (TEER). X-ray crystallography revealed that the lead barrier-weakening Nb, E6, binds to the membrane-proximal nondimeric D2 domain of mJAM-1. Mutating key residues at this interface eliminated the BBB-weakening effect of E6, as evidenced by unaltered sodium fluorescence (NaFI) leakage in both eGFP-hCldn5-MDCKII and mJAM1-mGL-MDCKII cellular monolayers compared with the nontreated control. Our study highlights the potential of JAM-1-targeting Nbs as BBB modulators, offering a promising approach for generating TJ binders to enhance brain drug delivery.

title: A Hyaluronic Acid-Stabilized Zinc-Loaded Probiotic Mitigates Nanoplastic Toxicity across the Microbiota-Gut-Brain Axis.
abstract: Nanoplastics are emerging stressors that perturb host physiology across the gut-immune-brain continuum, yet scalable interventions remain limited. Here, we engineer ZG@EcN@HA, a biohybrid living system created by vacuum-assisted intracellular loading of zinc gluconate into Escherichia coli Nissle 1917 (EcN) followed by an outer hyaluronic acid (HA) shell. This architecture preserves probiotic culturability under gastric challenge and supports sustained zinc availability in intestinal conditions. In zebrafish chronically exposed to polystyrene nanoplastics, we observe reproducible neurobehavioral impairment coupled with inflammatory activation, redox imbalance, barrier stress, neurotransmitter dysregulation, and multiorgan histopathology. ZG@EcN@HA yields the most coherent rescue compared with single-component controls, restoring behavioral outputs and realigning immune-redox-neurochemical readouts. ASV-based profiling shows recovery of microbial diversity and a shift toward a control-like community structure, including reduced dominance of inflammation-linked taxa. Intestinal transcriptomics and integrative correlation analyses further support normalization of barrier/metabolic programs and attenuation of innate inflammatory signaling. Together, the data identify a materials-enabled strategy for microbiota-gut-brain protection against chronic nanoplastic stress.

title: Disulfidptosis-Driven Immune-Activated Multimodal Therapy for Glioblastoma with Systemic Safety Control.
abstract: Effective glioblastoma therapy requires simultaneous solutions to poor blood-brain barrier (BBB) penetration, insufficient tumor-selective killing, and treatment-related systemic toxicity. We hypothesized that a BBB-penetrating nanoplatform capable of generating distinct H2S exposures in tumor and normal tissues could enhance antitumor efficacy while mitigating doxorubicin (DOX)-induced cardiotoxicity. Here, DOX-loaded metastable molybdenum disulfide nanoflowers functionalized with an I6P8 peptide (DOX@MSI) were developed. After BBB transport and tumor accumulation, the acidic, H2O2-rich, and GSH-rich microenvironment accelerates nanoplatform degradation, promoting GSH depletion and enhanced H2S/DOX release. High local H2S upregulates xCT, while H2S/DOX-mediated mitochondrial inhibition suppresses NADPH regeneration, synergistically triggering disulfidptosis. Meanwhile, H2S suppresses the JAK2/STAT3/IDO axis, alleviating DOX-induced immunosuppression and enhancing immunogenic cell death and T-cell-mediated antitumor immunity. In contrast, slower degradation under physiological conditions enables sustained low-level H2S release, reducing the level of oxidative stress and ERK-associated apoptosis in cardiomyocytes. Together with NIR-enhanced photothermal therapy, DOX@MSI suppresses orthotopic glioblastoma while reducing cardiac injury, thereby integrating tumor-selective multimodal therapy with active organ protection.

title: Near-Infrared Neuromodulation: Principles, Nanotechnology-Enabled Platforms, and Emerging Biomedical Frontiers.
abstract: Optogenetics enables highly specific regulation of neuronal activity with exceptional spatiotemporal precision, providing powerful tools for neural circuit interrogation and the treatment of neurological disorders. However, the limited tissue penetration of visible light restricts its application to deep neural tissues. Near-infrared (NIR) neuromodulation has emerged as a promising alternative by leveraging the superior tissue penetration and minimal invasiveness of NIR light. Recent advances in NIR-responsive nanomaterials, optical engineering, and neurotechnology have rapidly transformed the field from nonspecific photobiomodulation to cell-specific nanotransducer-mediated neuromodulation and integrated neuromodulation systems. In this review, we summarize the optical principles governing NIR propagation in biological tissues and the mechanisms underlying NIR-mediated neural stimulation. We then discuss recent advances in representative NIR nanotransducers, including photothermal, optoelectric, photoacoustic, and NIR-to-visible upconversion platforms together with integrated neuromodulation systems that combine NIR stimulation with multimodal neural recording and closed-loop feedback. We further highlight emerging applications in the central nervous system, optic nerve, and peripheral nerve disorders. Finally, we discuss the key challenges toward clinical translation, including improving tissue penetration, cell specificity, biosafety, and translation, developing intelligent multidisciplinary neuromodulation platforms, and integrating artificial intelligence with closed-loop neural interfaces to achieve adaptive, precise, and personalized neuromodulation.

title: Visible Light Modulates Macrophage Phenotype and Photoresponsive Carbon Monoxide Delivery.
abstract: Photoresponsive drug delivery systems are often described as bioorthogonal. However, certain wavelengths and intensities of visible light are known to modulate cellular phenotypes. This apparent discrepancy highlights a gap in knowledge with direct implications for the design of photoresponsive drug delivery systems. In this report, we investigated the response of primary macrophages to visible light (405-630 nm) due to their broad tissue distribution, phenotypic plasticity, and central role in orchestrating immune responses across diverse pathologies. We found distinct wavelength-dependent changes in cytochrome c oxidase activity, metabolic function, cytokine secretion, and biomarker expression at clinically relevant intensities of light. Further investigation of red light (630 nm) demonstrated complex dose-dependent metabolic and phenotypic responses. To illustrate the clinical implications of these findings, we employed 470 nm-triggerable carbon monoxide-releasing micelles to deconvolute the individual and combined effects of light exposure and therapeutic payloads. Our findings suggest that macrophages respond in a wavelength and intensity-dependent manner, and incorporating photoresponsive carbon monoxide-releasing systems elicits distinct immunomodulatory responses compared to irradiation alone. This work establishes a basic design framework for leveraging light parameters such as wavelength and intensity to achieve desirable immunomodulatory responses with photoresponsive drug delivery systems for specific disease applications.

title: German wine and respiration: Remarks on the discovery, properties and significance of the Bötzinger complex.
abstract: The Bötzinger complex (BötC) comprises a distinct bilateral group of interneurons that are active during the expiratory phase of the respiratory cycle, located in the rostral medulla ventral to the compact formation of the nucleus ambiguus. It was named after the bottles of wine served at the conference dinner of an international meeting held in Germany in 1980, where the first electrophysiological data describing these neurons were presented. In cats, BötC neurons predominantly exhibit an augmenting (E-Aug) firing pattern, whereas in rats E-Aug and E-Dec (decrementing expiratory) patterns are observed. Both subtypes issue axons that often extensively arborise on both sides of the medulla, forming inhibitory glycinergic and/or GABAergic synapses with inspiratory neurons of the dorsal and ventral respiratory groups. Additionally, E-Aug neurons project to the spinal cord and inhibit phrenic motoneurons. These properties contrast with those of another group of bulbospinal expiratory neurons in the caudal medulla, which do not issue medullary axon collaterals and are excitatory. BötC neurons regulate the interval during which inspiratory neurons remain silent and contribute to synchronisation of respiratory activity across both sides of the lower brainstem. Recent in vivo, reduced-preparation and in silico studies indicate that they also contribute to respiratory rhythmogenesis through mutual inhibitory synaptic interactions with the pre-Bötzinger complex. This review provides the history of the discovery and naming of the BötC and a detailed discussion of the properties of BötC neurons, including their location, morphology, afferent and efferent axonal projections, synaptic connectivity and functional role.

title: Toward a Tonic-Phasic Framework for Understanding Parenting and Child Irritability: a Narrative Review.
journal: Clinical child and family psychology review
abstract: Irritability is among the most prevalent and impairing transdiagnostic features of child and adolescent psychopathology. Despite growing recognition of its public health significance, the field has been constrained by two related problems: a tendency to treat irritability as a unitary construct, and a near-total absence of attention to the caregiving contexts in which irritability develops and is maintained. This developmental review addresses these gaps by: (1) synthesizing converging evidence that tonic and phasic irritability represent related but empirically non-redundant dimensions, that is, they share meaningful variance but show partially distinct developmental trajectories, clinical correlates, and prognostic implications; (2) organizing the parenting literature by mapping specific caregiving processes onto tonic versus phasic pathways, distinguishing parenting practices from parenting-adjacent constructs that are analytically and conceptually distinct from parenting but may shape irritability through both parenting-mediated and other family-contextual pathways; and (3) proposing a developmental-transactional model grounded in developmental psychopathology principles that specifies how child vulnerabilities, parenting processes, and contextual stressors interact over time to produce chronic irritable mood versus episodic anger. Clinical implications and future directions are discussed.

title: The Gut-Brain Axis in Binge Eating Disorder: From Pathophysiological Mechanisms to Emerging Therapeutic Targets.
abstract: Binge-eating disorder (BED) is one of the most prevalent eating disorders worldwide; however, current pharmacological and psychological interventions provide limited long-term efficacy. Increasing evidence indicates that dysregulation of the gut-brain axis (GBA) via altered gut microbiota, impaired hormonal signaling, vagal dysfunction, and HPA axis hyperactivity disrupts energy homeostasis and feeding regulation in BED. These interconnected abnormalities may contribute to impaired satiety perception, enhance reward-driven eating behaviors, perpetuate stress-induced binge episodes, and may be associated with metabolic dysregulation, thereby contributing to obesity susceptibility in individuals with BED. In this review, we summarize recent clinical and preclinical advances on GBA involvement in BED pathogenesis and discuss emerging therapeutic strategies targeting this regulatory network. We pay particular attention to microbial metabolites, endocrine signaling, immune regulation, and neural pathways involved in appetite control and reward processing. Furthermore, we evaluate novel GBA-targeted interventions, including probiotics, prebiotics, fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT), glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor (GLP-1R) agonists, and vagus nerve stimulation (VNS), with emphasis on their underlying mechanisms, current evidence, and translational challenges. Finally, we propose an integrated framework for future research, highlighting the importance of large-scale longitudinal studies and biomarker-guided patient stratification to improve therapeutic precision. Targeting the gut-brain axis represents a promising investigational approach for BED management; however, clinical validation and biomarker-guided strategies remain necessary before its translation into routine practice.

title: Correction to: Range-Limited Scale Stability of Dynamic Direction Representations in a Connectome-Constrained Fly Visual Model.
Retraction Note to: Repeated Forced Swim Exacerbates Methamphetamine-Induced Neurotoxicity: Neuroprotective Effects of Nanowired Delivery of 5-HT3-Receptor Antagonist Ondansetron.
Preferences of Patients with Type 1 Diabetes for Glucose Monitoring Devices: Results from a Discrete Choice Experiment in the UK and Canada.
abstract: Regular self-monitoring of glucose levels is integral to diabetes management to achieve glycaemic control and reduce the risk of acute and long-term complications. Wearable glucose monitoring devices provide more comprehensive information on glucose fluctuations than traditional finger-prick testing. However, access restrictions contribute to inequalities in adoption. This study elicited the preferences of patients with type 1 diabetes in the UK and Canada for attributes of glucose monitoring devices. An online discrete choice experiment was conducted among adults (aged ≥ 18 years) with type 1 diabetes. Respondents chose between standard finger-prick testing (usual care) and two hypothetical glucose monitoring devices described using six attributes: convenience of monitoring, time lag, level of information, alarm to signal low and high glucose levels, glycated haemoglobin level and time in range, and an out-of-pocket monthly cost. Responses were analysed using a mixed logit model, and marginal willingness to pay was calculated. A pooled model using country interaction terms was used to formally compare preferences across countries. The discrete choice experiment was completed by 112 UK and 102 Canadian respondents. Across countries, respondents preferred devices offering convenience, alarm capabilities, real-time glucose readings and more comprehensive glucose information. Preferences were broadly consistent across countries, with only preferences for alarm functionality differing significantly. However, substantial preference heterogeneity was observed within both countries, indicating variation in the device characteristics valued by individuals. Overall, the discrete choice experiment results indicate that adults with type 1 diabetes preferred characteristics relating to the newer glucose monitoring devices. Substantial variation in individual preferences suggests that access to a range of glucose monitoring devices may be important to accommodate differences in the characteristics patients value.

title: Association of GLP-1 receptor agonist use with mortality and healthcare utilization in patients with vascular dementia.
abstract: Patients with vascular dementia (VD) have high mortality and frequent acute care use, and no treatment has been shown to improve these outcomes. Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) are associated with a lower incidence of dementia and with cardiovascular benefit in type 2 diabetes, but their association with clinical outcomes in patients with established VD is unknown. This retrospective cohort study using a national database identified patients with VD from 2016 to 2025. Patients receiving GLP-1RAs within one month of diagnosis were propensity-score matched with non-users (n = 613 per group). Primary outcome was mortality at 1, 3, and 5 years; secondary outcomes included hospitalizations and emergency visits. GLP-1RA use was associated with lower risk of mortality at 1 year (8.7% vs. 15.9%; HR 0.49, 95% CI 0.34-0.71), 3 years (23.3% vs. 33.8%; HR 0.58, 95% CI 0.44-0.76), and 5 years (34.4% vs. 54.3%; HR 0.53, 95% CI 0.41-0.69) (all p < 0.001). In addition, GLP-1RA use was associated with lower risk of inpatient admissions and emergency visits. GLP-1RA use in patients with VD was associated with lower risk of mortality and healthcare utilization. These beneficial associations warrant prospective randomized trials.

title: Platelet lysates ameliorate impaired neuronal autophagy in Parkinson's Disease: correlative evidence for ROS/Akt signaling.
abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is the second most common neurodegenerative disorder and represents a growing global health challenge. Platelet lysates (PLs) are enriched in growth factors, cytokines, and bioactive proteins with known tissue-regenerative and neurorestorative properties; however, their neuroprotective efficacy and molecular mechanisms in PD remain unclear. This study aimed to investigate the neuroprotective effects of PLs in PD models and to explore the underlying mechanisms. SH-SY5Y cells exposed to 6-OHDA, MPP⁺, or rotenone were used as in vitro PD models. Cell viability, morphological injury, ROS levels, TH expression, and p-α-syn (Ser129) levels were assessed. Autophagosome formation was evaluated using an Ad-GFP-LC3 transduction assay, and autophagic flux was further verified by bafilomycin A1-mediated lysosomal blockade. Mechanistic studies employed SC79 (Akt activator) and N-acetylcysteine (NAC, ROS scavenger). In vivo, MPTP-induced and A53T transgenic mouse models of PD were used to evaluate nigrostriatal dopaminergic neuronal protection, Nissl body preservation, p-α-syn accumulation, and motor function. PLs ameliorated neurotoxin-induced morphological injury, increased cell viability, reduced intracellular ROS levels, upregulated TH expression, and decreased p-α-syn (Ser129) accumulation in SH-SY5Y cells. Ad-GFP-LC3 assays showed that PLs promoted autophagosome biogenesis, and bafilomycin A1-based flux assays further confirmed that PLs rescued neurotoxin-impaired autophagic flux across all three toxin models. Mechanistically, PLs consistently reduced ROS and enhanced Akt phosphorylation. In MPP⁺- and 6-OHDA-injured cells, this was accompanied by ATG5/LC3-II upregulation and restoration of autophagic degradation; however, in the rotenone model, the toxin-induced ATG5 reduction was not significantly reversed despite effective attenuation of oxidative stress and p62 accumulation, suggesting ATG5-independent protective mechanisms. In vivo, PLs administration protected nigrostriatal dopaminergic neurons, preserved Nissl bodies, reduced p-α-syn (Ser129) immunoreactivity, and improved motor function in both MPTP-induced and A53T transgenic mouse models of PD. PLs attenuate neurotoxin-induced neuronal injury and improve pathological and behavioral phenotypes in PD models. The ROS/Akt signaling axis appears to be one plausible mechanistic correlate of PLs-mediated neuroprotection, with toxin-specific divergence in downstream autophagy mechanisms. These findings support further investigation of PLs as a potential intervention for PD-related pathological phenotypes.

title: Mapping intratumoral coverage of neural stem cell-delivered anti-HER2 antibody in breast cancer brain metastasis.
abstract: Cell-based therapies can formulate and deliver biologics within the brain, but their development has relied largely on survival outcomes that do not distinguish inadequate payload potency from inadequate tumor distribution. We evaluated intratumoral coverage as a quantitative endpoint for cell-mediated delivery using neural stem cells (NSCs) engineered to secrete an anti-HER2 antibody in breast cancer brain metastasis. Intracranial HER2-positive BT474Br tumors received a single dose of 5 × 105 anti-HER2 antibody-secreting NSCs. Secreted human IgG was reconstructed across consecutive 10-µm sections spanning the entire tumor depth, and therapeutic activity of the same cell dose administered once was assessed in an independent survival experiment. A single NSC dose produced a mean section-level antibody coverage of 60.6%; coverage was ≥ 25% in 96.8% of sections and ≥ 50% in 74.2%. Coverage was greatest in the tumor core and declined toward both poles, a pattern consistent with carrier-cell localization limiting therapeutic reach. The same dose extended median survival from 67 days with vector-control NSCs to 73.5 days (P = 0.0009) and increased restricted mean survival by 10.8 days. These data provide an initial spatial benchmark for a therapeutically active dose and establish tumor coverage as a mechanistically informative endpoint for intracranial cell-based delivery.

title: Distinct sympathoneural and cardiovagal domains of arterial baroreflex function in autonomic synucleinopathies.
journal: Clinical autonomic research : official journal of the Clinical Autonomic Research Society
abstract: The arterial baroreflex has sympathoneural and cardiovagal efferent limbs. Whether quantitative measures represent interchangeable indicators of a single physiological construct has been unclear. Moreover, the extent to which results agree in the synucleinopathies pure autonomic failure (PAF), Parkinson disease with or without orthostatic hypotension (PD + OH, PD No OH), and multiple system atrophy (MSA) remains incompletely understood. In a retrospective observational study we comprehensively assessed physiological and neurochemical biomarkers of arterial baroreflex function in these disorders. Data for 10 baroreflex-sympathoneural and 6 baroreflex-cardiovagal indices were compared among 38 patients with PAF, 63 with PD + OH, 63 with PD No OH, and 72 with MSA, along with a pooled Control group (130 total; 44 with complete autonomic baroreflex datasets). Indices of baroreflex-sympathoneural and baroreflex-cardiovagal function were only weakly correlated. Within the two domains, correlations across subjects were much stronger. Among sympathoneural measures, pressure recovery time after the Valsalva maneuver, the logarithm of the total baroreflex area, and the fractional orthostatic increment in plasma norepinephrine best distinguished patients with autonomic synucleinopathies from controls. Among cardiovagal measures, the Baroslope derived from Phase II of the Valsalva maneuver and the logarithms of low- and high-frequency heart rate variability during supine rest were the most informative. No baroreflex measure separated PAF from PD + OH or MSA. Indices derived from blood pressure and interbeat interval responses during the Valsalva maneuver capture much of the physiologically meaningful variation in baroreflex function and enable efficient assessment of the sympathoneural and cardiovagal limbs in autonomic synucleinopathies.

title: Diagnostic and prognostic biomarkers for pediatric cerebral malaria: a review.
abstract: Pediatric cerebral malaria (PCM) kills 15% to 25% of the African children in whom it is diagnosed and leaves many survivors with neurocognitive deficits. It is a disease of the cerebral microvasculature whose pathogenic sequence is now partly resolved at the molecular level. Plasmodium falciparum erythrocyte membrane protein 1 binds a broad range of endothelial cell receptors, of which binding to the endothelial protein C receptor, in some cases together with intercellular adhesion molecule 1, is the combination linked to severe and cerebral disease. CD36 is the receptor most commonly used by field isolates but is associated with uncomplicated malaria, at least two dozen further receptors have been described for parasitized erythrocytes, and a PfEMP1 binding domain has been identified for only a few of them. The ensuing endothelial activation releases von Willebrand factor and angiopoietin-2 and disables Tie - 2 signaling. Free heme, delivered in part by histidine-rich protein 2 nanoparticles internalized by caveolin-1-dependent endocytosis, is proposed to engage two separable innate arms, one through stimulator of interferon genes 1 (STING1) yielding type I interferon and CXCL10, the other through NLRP3 and caspase - 1 yielding interleukin-1-beta; the first was shown in murine brain endothelium and the second in a human cerebral endothelial cell line, and the two have not been demonstrated in one system. Junctional remodeling and ephrin type-A receptor 2 signaling open the blood-brain barrier in murine models, barrier disruption is documented histologically in human autopsy series, and neuronal and axonal proteins reach the circulation of affected children. The sequence summarized here therefore combines links established in human disease with links that remain experimental or proposed, and the review marks which is which at each step. This review treats candidate biomarkers as readouts of that cascade rather than as free-standing correlates. Because the clinical definition cannot separate malaria-attributable coma from coma with incidental parasitemia, we appraise malarial retinopathy as the in vivo reference standard and set out why a negative result is heterogeneous. Parasite-derived and host-derived markers are mapped onto those steps, with attention to the few evaluated against non-malarial coma rather than against milder malaria, and to what a marker adds at the bedside. Extracellular vesicles and microRNAs are assessed as emerging platforms. We close on druggable nodes in the cascade and on using molecular readouts to stratify children for host-directed therapy.

title: Intranasal nanocarrier-based drug delivery in multiple sclerosis: therapeutic cargo, CNS targeting and translational challenges.
abstract: Efficiently delivering therapeutics to the central nervous system (CNS) remains a major challenge in multiple sclerosis (MS), particularly for strategies targeting CNS-resident pathology, neuroprotection, or remyelination. This review provides a delivery- and formulation-centered comparative analysis of CNS drug delivery strategies for MS, integrating administration route, nanocarrier design, evidence level, and translational feasibility within a unified framework. A structured narrative review was conducted using literature identified through PubMed, Scopus, and Google Scholar, encompassing conventional and alternative administration routes, including intranasal (IN) delivery, and lipid-based, polymeric, and hybrid nanocarrier systems. Strategies were evaluated using predefined criteria, including BBB permeability or CNS exposure, targeting capability, bioavailability, formulation characteristics, and translational feasibility. A semi-quantitative heatmap based on a predefined ordinal scoring system and available experimental and clinical evidence was developed to enable transparent comparison. Conventional systemic administration may be limited by systemic exposure, first-pass metabolism, and restricted CNS access. IN administration is a promising investigational approach to enhance CNS exposure for selected compounds; however, evidence for direct nose-to-brain (N2B) transport depends on the drug, formulation, and experimental model. Nanocarriers can improve solubility and stability, protect against degradation, enable controlled release, and may enhance CNS exposure or cellular targeting in selected preclinical settings. Nevertheless, evidence for BBB penetration, direct CNS targeting, and therapeutic efficacy remains predominantly preclinical, with limited standardized pharmacokinetic and clinical validation. Overall, the comparative framework highlights the importance of jointly considering administration route, nanocarrier properties, and evidence maturity to guide rational CNS delivery design and future translational development in MS.

title: A green approach to treating neurological conditions: the promise of plant-derived exosome-like nanovesicles.
abstract: Plant-derived exosome-like nanovesicles (PELNs) are being investigated as bioactive preparations and drug carriers for neurological disorders. However, preparations recovered from disrupted plant tissues are heterogeneous and should not automatically be equated with naturally secreted extracellular vesicles or endosome-derived exosomes. This narrative review critically examines vesicle identity, isolation and purification, cellular uptake, brain delivery, disease-specific evidence, and translational requirements. Ultracentrifugation, size exclusion chromatography, polymer precipitation, and microfluidic approaches offer different trade-offs between recovery, contaminant removal, throughput, and scalability. Preclinical studies report effects in ischemic injury, glioma, amyloid-related models, Parkinsonian models, and gut-brain signaling, but these findings depend on the plant source, formulation, administration route, and experimental model. Endothelial uptake, transport across an intact blood-brain barrier, entry through a damaged barrier, and intranasal delivery represent distinct processes. Fluorescent tissue accumulation alone does not establish delivery of intact vesicles or functional cargo. Recent negative and cell-selective findings further challenge the assumption that all PELNs are effective neuronal carriers. Clinical development requires quantitative pharmacokinetics, route-specific biodistribution, repeated-dose safety assessment, causal cargo validation, and reproducible manufacturing with potency-linked release specifications. PELNs therefore provide a promising research platform rather than an established class of safe, intrinsically brain-targeting therapeutics. Their proposed environmental and commercial advantages also require direct process, cost, and life-cycle evaluation.

title: Carbonyl stress as the missing molecular link between diabetes and neurodegeneration: a unified mechanistic framework for type 3 diabetes.
abstract: Type 2 diabetes mellitus is associated with an increased risk of cognitive dysfunction and neurodegenerative changes, contributing to the emerging concept of "Type 3 Diabetes," characterized by impaired cerebral insulin signaling and altered brain glucose metabolism.
