However, the metabolic processes connecting systemic metabolic dysfunction with cerebral insulin resistance remain incompletely understood. This review examines carbonyl stress, particularly methylglyoxal and other reactive dicarbonyls, as potential links between dysregulated glucose metabolism and impaired cerebral insulin signaling. We evaluate MGO generation and glyoxalase-mediated detoxification, evidence linking carbonyl stress with insulin-signaling abnormalities and interactions among AGE-RAGE signaling, oxidative stress and neuroinflammation. Particular emphasis is placed on distinguishing evidence from peripheral insulin-responsive tissues, vascular compartments and neuronal models, given the limited direct in vivo evidence establishing MGO as a cause of cerebral insulin resistance. The review further considers potential consequences for neuronal metabolism, synaptic function, and neurodegenerative vulnerability, alongside emerging therapeutic strategies targeting carbonyl metabolism and related pathways, including intranasal nanocarrier-mediated delivery. Overall, carbonyl stress represents a biologically plausible but not yet established molecular link between diabetes-associated metabolic dysfunction and neurodegenerative vulnerability, warranting brain-specific studies to determine its causal and therapeutic relevance.

title: Susceptibility-weighted imaging findings in subacute sclerosing panencephalitis: subcortical paramagnetic rim and deep gray matter changes.
abstract: Subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder caused by persistent measles virus infection. Conventional MRI plays a key role in diagnosis and staging; however, susceptibility-weighted imaging (SWI) findings in SSPE have not been systematically characterized, particularly with respect to their relationship to disease burden and neurodegeneration. With this study we aim to evaluate SWI changes in SSPE, with emphasis on the Subcortical Paramagnetic Rim (SPR) and deep gray matter mineralization, and to assess their association with parenchymal disease burden and cerebral atrophy. This retrospective single-center study included 126 patients with confirmed SSPE who underwent MRI including SWI. T2/FLAIR hyperintensities were assessed across predefined supratentorial and infratentorial parenchymal regions. A composite total parenchymal disease burden score was calculated. Cerebral atrophy and deep gray matter mineralization were evaluated using semi-quantitative visual grading systems. SWI was also assessed for the presence of a SPR. Associations between susceptibility findings, parenchymal disease burden, cerebral atrophy, and clinical parameters were analyzed using non-parametric statistical methods. SPR was identified in 14 of 128 MRI studies (10.9%), most commonly involving the parietal lobes. Patients with the rim had significantly longer symptom duration, higher disease stage, greater parenchymal disease burden, higher atrophy scores, and higher deep gray matter mineralization scores compared with patients without the rim (p < 0.01). Deep gray matter mineralization scores showed significant positive correlations with both global parenchymal disease burden and cerebral atrophy (Spearman's ρ, p < 0.001). SPR and deep gray matter mineralization, are associated with increasing parenchymal disease burden and atrophy. These findings likely represent imaging markers of disease chronicity and provide complementary information to conventional MRI, particularly in the evaluation of chronic encephalitis in measles-endemic regions.

title: Alcohol and Opioids Modulate Excitatory Inputs to the SCN.
abstract: Disturbance of circadian rhythms is a hallmark of substance use disorders, with depressant drugs often causing soporific effects such as reduced sleep latency. The suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) of the hypothalamus is the central circadian pacemaker in mammals, regulating daily rhythms in physiology and behavior. However, the cellular mechanisms through which depressants alter SCN function remain poorly defined. We used whole-cell patch clamp electrophysiology in coronal brain slices to examine how alcohol and opioids modulate excitatory glutamatergic transmission onto SCN neurons. Ethanol effects were examined acutely and following chronic exposure paradigms. Optogenetic stimulation was used to activate either retinohypothalamic tract (RHT) input or μ-opioid receptor-expressing (MOR+) terminals, and MOR agonists were used to assess opioid-mediated effects on synaptic transmission. We show that acute application of ethanol enhances SCN firing rates during the inactive locomotor stage of circadian rhythms (daytime for rodents). In contrast, chronic alcohol exposure reduces glutamatergic drive. We also found that activating MOR+ terminals via an excitatory channelrhodopsin transgenically expressed in MOR+ neurons produced bidirectional modulation of SCN firing and that MOR+ inputs formed functional glutamatergic synapses onto SCN neurons. We also found that chronic alcohol consumption significantly altered MOR-dependent modulation of SCN neuronal activity, demonstrating an interaction between ethanol exposure and opioidergic signaling. Notably, MOR-mediated transmission could be suppressed by the MOR agonists DAMGO and fentanyl. Together, these findings reveal that both alcohol and opioids modulate glutamatergic input to the SCN. This work establishes the SCN as a novel target of depressant substances and highlights glutamatergic transmission as a key point of vulnerability in circadian dysregulation associated with substance use.

title: Lysergic Acid Diethylamide Induces Transcriptional Changes Opposing Signatures of Brain Ageing and Neurodegeneration.
abstract: Psychedelic compounds such as lysergic acid diethylamide (LSD) are increasingly studied for their neuroplastic effects and potential relevance to brain ageing and neurodegenerative conditions, including dementia. These processes are characterised by transcriptional changes involving progressive synaptic dysfunction and altered neuron-glia interactions. In computational drug discovery, the transcriptional signature reversion principle proposes that compounds inducing gene expression states opposite to disease-associated programmes may have therapeutic potential by counteracting disease-associated phenotypes. We therefore asked whether LSD-induced transcriptional changes oppose gene expression programmes associated with brain ageing and dementia, thereby providing a data-driven rationale for its potential relevance to age-associated cognitive decline and a starting point for investigating the underlying molecular mechanisms. Combining cross-species transcriptomic analyses with experimental validation, we show that transcriptional profiles induced by chronic LSD treatment in rats are strongly anti-correlated with ageing-associated gene expression changes in the human prefrontal cortex and, to a lesser extent, with dementia-associated programmes. This relationship is reproducible across datasets and species and is significantly stronger compared to a broad panel of pharmacological perturbations. Independent acute LSD treatment in mice recapitulated the opposition to ageing-associated transcriptional signatures across multiple doses. Moreover, short-term LSD treatment attenuated amyloid-β-induced structural, molecular and transcriptional alterations in primary cortical cultures. Together, these findings provide a transcriptionally grounded rationale for investigating LSD and related compounds in brain ageing and neurodegeneration, while identifying molecular and cellular programmes that can guide future mechanistic and therapeutic studies.

title: The Effect of Natural Compounds on Cognitive Impairment Through BDNF/TrkB/CREB Pathway: A Review.
abstract: Considering the global prevalence of Alzheimer's disease (AD) and the restrictions of current treatment procedures, natural compounds (such as curcumin, hesperidin, and rutin) have been evaluated as multifaceted therapeutic agents. This review demonstrated that these compounds employ neuroprotective effects primarily through upregulating the brain-derived neurotrophic factor/tropomyosin receptor kinase B/cAMP response element binding protein (BDNF/TrkB/CREB) pathway. After inducing this pathway, they subsequently decrease apoptosis through the regulation of B-cell lymphoma protein 2-associated X/B-cell lymphoma 2 protein (Bax/Bcl2) ratio and the inhibition of apoptosis signal-regulating kinase 1 (ASK1) (e.g., icariin). They also modulate oxidative stress via increasing superoxide dismutase, catalase, and glutathione peroxidase (e.g., hesperidin), and suppress neuroinflammation through the inhibition of nuclear factor kappa-light-chain-enhancer of activated B cells (Nf-κB) and proinflammatory cytokines (e.g., curcumin). These compounds enhance the level of postsynaptic density protein (PSD-95), a key enhancer of neuronal plasticity, improve synaptic signaling (e.g., oleanolic acid), and reduce cognitive disorders by reducing the formation of amyloid beta (Aβ) plaques (e.g., rutin). The phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase/protein kinase B (PI3K/Akt) signaling pathway is modulated (e.g., icariin), and cholinergic neurons are restored (e.g., maslinic acid). Despite the beneficial potential of natural compounds, the extrapolation of their findings to clinical application requires more precise preclinical studies and validated biomarkers.

title: Corrigendum to "Good communication with adults with learning disabilities in long-term care settings: A realist review" [Disabil Health J 19 (2026) 102078].
Development and Psychometric Evaluation of the Videolaryngoscopy and Stroboscopy Reporting Tool (VSRT).
journal: Journal of voice : official journal of the Voice Foundation
abstract: Effective diagnosis and treatment of voice/laryngeal disorders depend on comprehensive assessments, among which direct visual evaluation of the larynx primarily via videolaryngoscopy and videostroboscopy is a cornerstone. The main issue with these evaluations is that they only provide complex, uninterpreted images. However, for clinical diagnosis, treatment outcome assessment, and even higher-level voice research, well-defined, standardized, and quantifiable parameters are required. Therefore, the aim of this study was to develop a comprehensive, valid, and reliable tool for reporting the results of videolaryngoscopy and videostroboscopy of the larynx. This tool can help to provide more effective treatment and establish a common language in instrumental assessments. The study was conducted in two phases: (1) tool development through a review of existing scientific and expert consultation (input from the research team), resulting in the initial version of the Videolaryngoscopy and Stroboscopy Reporting Tool (VSRT); and (2) psychometric evaluation was conducted, including both quantitative and qualitative assessments of content validity using the opinions of experts active in the field of voice/laryngeal disorder evaluation and treatment, qualitative face validity via interviews with speech-language pathologists, otolaryngologists, and laryngologists, and reliability evaluation through intra-rater and inter-rater reliability methods. The first phase of the study resulted in the development of an initial tool with 19 items. After evaluating the qualitative content validity by the experts, the number of tool items increased to 20. Following content validation, guide images were added to some items, and the scoring method for some items was modified. No items were removed during the content validity ratio and content validity index determination, as all items met the predefined inclusion criteria. In the face validity stage, explanations were added to some items to facilitate completion based on feedback to enhance usability. The intra-rater reliability ranged from 0.644 to 0.986 (categorical items) and 0.456 to 0.991 (numeric items); inter-rater reliability ranged from 0.238 to 0.814 (categorical items) and 0.609 to 0.893 (numeric items). The VSRT is a standardized 20-item instrument for reporting videolaryngoscopy and stroboscopy findings. Its psychometric properties support its utility in clinical and research contexts, offering improved clarity, interpretability, treatment planning, and consistency across interdisciplinary teams.

title: Functional brain signatures of successful cognitive aging.
abstract: Cognitive aging trajectories vary markedly. While many older adults experience gradual decline in memory and executive function, some maintain high cognitive performance well into advanced age. Understanding the neural mechanisms underlying this variability carries important implications for early detection of unfavorable aging trajectories and the development of interventions. Here, we review functional brain signatures associated with successful cognitive aging in humans, integrating evidence from functional magnetic resonance imaging and electroencephalography within a unified conceptual framework of brain maintenance and compensation. Across both modalities, evidence increasingly links successful cognitive aging to the preservation of youth-like neural dynamics, while the contribution of compensatory neural recruitment remains empirically contested and methodologically difficult to establish.

title: Comb-Like EEG Pattern as an Early Diagnostic Clue in Maple Syrup Urine Disease (MSUD): A Systematic Review.
journal: American journal of medical genetics. Part A
abstract: Maple syrup urine disease (MSUD) is a life-threatening inborn error of amino acid metabolism that often presents in the neonatal period with nonspecific symptoms such as poor feeding, lethargy, and seizures. Although newborn screening (NBS) enables early identification, false-negative results and delays in reporting may lead to missed or delayed diagnosis, resulting in severe neurologic injury. A characteristic EEG finding, the "comb-like rhythm," consisting of central- or frontocentral-predominant, sharply contoured 4-7 Hz theta bursts has been reported in MSUD. However, its diagnostic utility has not been systematically evaluated. Therefore, we aimed to investigate the comb-like rhythm as a diagnostic clue for MSUD. A systematic literature search was conducted in accordance with PRISMA guidelines using MEDLINE and Embase databases up to May 18, 2026. Studies evaluating EEG findings in individuals with MSUD were included. Data on clinical presentation, biochemical findings, brain imaging, and EEG features were extracted and synthesized qualitatively. In addition, two neonatal cases from our institution were included. Associations of the comb-like EEG rhythm with patient age at EEG (neonatal vs. non-neonatal) and plasma leucine concentrations were evaluated using Fisher's exact test and the Mann-Whitney U test. A total of 113 records were screened, and 18 studies were included, comprising 24 symptomatic cases including our two patients. Abnormal EEG findings were reported in 21 of 24 (88%). A comb-like pattern was exclusively observed in neonates with acute metabolic crisis (13/15 neonates [86.7%] vs. 0/9 non-neonates [0%], p < 0.0001). The comb-like rhythm was associated with higher plasma leucine concentrations (median, 3545 vs. 1782 μmol/L, p = 0.0033). The pattern often diminished or resolved following treatment or clinical stabilization. In our two patients, the comb-like rhythm contributed to raising diagnostic suspicion despite initially normal NBS results. The comb-like rhythm may serve as an adjunctive EEG marker that raises suspicion for acute MSUD, given its strong association with neonatal metabolic crisis and severe hyperleucinemia. Further studies are needed to clarify its pathophysiological basis and determine the clinical utility of EEG in MSUD crisis.

title: The association of intrapartum oral labetalol for preeclampsia with severe features and risk of cesarean delivery: a retrospective cohort study.
journal: The journal of maternal-fetal & neonatal medicine : the official journal of the European Association of Perinatal Medicine, the Federation of Asia and Oceania Perinatal Societies, the International Society of Perinatal Obstetricians
abstract: To evaluate if the use of intrapartum oral labetalol vs. no antihypertensive medication additions for severe preeclampsia (PreE with SF) for sustained oral blood pressure control decreases the risk of cesarean. This was a retrospective cohort study of patients who underwent a trial of labor of a non-anomalous, singleton gestation at ≥ 34 weeks gestational age with preeclampsia with severe features. The exposure was intrapartum oral labetalol compared to no oral antihypertensive medication. The use of intrapartum labetalol was defined as the initiation of labetalol in labor for preeclampsia with severe features. The primary outcome was the need for cesarean. Univariable analyses were performed to evaluate the association of oral labetalol therapy and need for cesarean. Variables that had an independent association with the outcome were determined a priori and included in the multivariable regression analysis. Statistical significance was defined as p < 0.05. 642 patients met the inclusion criteria. A total of 134 patients (20.9%) received intrapartum oral labetalol, whereas 508 (79.1%) were not started on antihypertensive medications. Patients who were initiated on oral labetalol in labor for blood pressure control were significantly more likely to have a lower gestational age at delivery (35.0 vs 37.7 weeks gestation, p < 0.001) and have a higher risk of needing IV antihypertensives in labor (95.5 vs 80.6%, p < 0.001). There were no other statistically significant baseline differences between groups. 62 (46.3%) individuals in the labetalol group and 192 (37.8%) in the no antihypertensives group underwent cesarean section. In multivariable analysis of the primary outcome, patients who were started on oral labetalol in labor were not at an increased risk of cesarean (aOR 1.32, 95% CI 0.88-1.99). Composite adverse neonatal outcomes were higher in the oral labetalol group and more patients in the oral labetalol group required cesarean for worsening preeclampsia and abnormal fetal heart tones. Intrapartum oral labetalol use was not associated with a significant difference in cesarean rates. Univariable analysis suggests a higher odds of composite adverse neonatal outcomes as well as differing indications for cesarean sections, however, this is likely secondary to confounding by indication.

title: Mitochondrial protein import stress augments α-synuclein aggregation and neural damage.
abstract: Genetic and environmental factors are known to converge on mitochondria to cause Parkinson's disease. The underlying mechanism is incompletely understood. In addition to bioenergetic defects, nonbioenergetic pathways have been largely unexplored. Validating the nonbioenergetic mitochondrial stressors as independent pathogenic factors is challenging because most mouse models of mitochondrial stress are confounded by bioenergetic defects. Here, we show that expression of Ant1P.A114P,A123D, previously shown to cause mitochondrial protein import clogging in cultured human cells, does not affect the overall bioenergetic capacity, yet it induces proteostatic stress responses in the cytosol that suggests accumulation of unimported precursor proteins. In a Parkinson's disease model expressing α-synuclein (A53T), Ant1P.A114P,A123D increased the size of α-synuclein aggregates, increased aggregation of mitochondrial preproteins, heightened neuroinflammation, and worsened motor coordination defects. Importantly, we found no evidence of bioenergetic defects in either α-synuclein (A53T) or α-synuclein (A53T) + Ant1P.A114P,A123D mice. These data suggest that Ant1P.A114P,A123D likely induces mitochondrial protein import stress, and contributes to neural damage through cytosolic proteostatic stress and altered aggregation dynamics of neuropathogenic proteins independent of bioenergetics.

title: From preconception risk to perinatal outcomes: machine learning prediction of depression and acute psychiatric care from electronic health records in the UK.
Deciphering the molecular granularity of subependymomas and its distinction from posterior fossa ependymoma.
abstract: The CNS tumor classification of the WHO currently subsumes subependymomas (SE) of the supratentorial, infratentorial, and spinal compartment as one tumor type. Molecular data on SE are generally sparse, but SE are known to exhibit distinct global DNA methylation profiles according to their anatomical location. Previous studies indicate that a fraction of posterior fossa tumors exhibiting DNA methylation profiles of SE morphologically appear as ependymomas and may be prone to relapse. We assembled a cohort of ependymal tumors that best match supratentorial (n = 89), infratentorial (n = 146), or spinal (n = 45) SE DNA methylation profiles. Infratentorial tumors with an SE DNA methylation profile occurred at significantly higher ages with a male to female ratio of 4:1 and displayed two distinct subtypes. One of them (n = 49) was enriched for tumors that morphologically appear as ependymomas, carrying a loss of chromosome 6 as well as TERT promoter mutations. Respective patients showed a significantly shorter progression-free survival (p = 0.00014). Supratentorial SE frequently showed chromosome 8 loss while a small subset of tumors with a distinct DNA methylation profile and a segmentation of chromosome 6 was detected. Such chromosomal abnormalities were similarly observed in spinal SE. Based on clustering analysis and clinical features of tumors best matching a subependymoma methylation class, we postulate four subtypes of subependymomas. A fifth, previously undefined type of infratentorial ependymomas was provisionally named PFC. It showed frequent relapses but was distinct from PFA and PFB ependymomas.

title: Mirroring emotional faces: Functional connectivity of the Mirror Neuron System in young children and adults.
abstract: The Mirror Neuron System (MNS) underlies important neurocognitive functions, such as imitation learning, social cognition and empathy, and may facilitate the recognition of emotional expressions via motor simulation. However, its development remains poorly understood. This study investigated functional connectivity maturation of MNS-related areas between early childhood and adulthood during an emotional faces task. Using the innovative magnetoencephalography approach of optically pumped magnetometers (OPMs), we assessed whole-brain connectivity with 8 bilateral regions of interest (ROIs), representing the MNS, in 57 typically developing children aged 3-to-5 years and 27 adults. We applied both classical network-based statistic (NBS) and its more recent approach incorporating machine learning, NBS-Predict. We observed networks of increased connectivity after face presentation in both adults and children in broadband, as well as in the alpha and beta bands; only adults recruited a theta band network. The networks included connections between MNS ROIs and key limbic, prefrontal, parietal and occipital areas. Notably, adults exhibited a network of increased connectivity in broadband and theta band, with a trend towards right-lateralisation compared to children. Results were validated with NBS-Predict, with a comparable subnetwork exhibiting predictive features for classification between children and adults. Our findings suggest that the network involving MNS ROIs during observation of facial expressions evolves between early childhood and adulthood, consistent with right-hemisphere specialisation in emotional processing.

title: Older adults' experiences of participating in longitudinal ageing research: a qualitative study from the Swedish National study on Aging and Care in Kungsholmen.
Cognitive Behavioural Therapy to Optimize Post-Operative Fracture Recovery (COPE): a randomized controlled trial.
journal: CMAJ : Canadian Medical Association journal = journal de l'Association medicale canadienne
abstract: Persistent pain after extremity fracture requiring surgical repair is common and associated with long-term morbidity. We sought to determine whether app-based cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) reduces persistent postsurgical pain after fracture repair. We performed a randomized controlled trial of adults from 11 American and Canadian hospitals with an extremity fracture treated with internal fixation. We allocated participants 1:1 to an app-based CBT program or usual care, and followed them at 3, 6, 9, and 12 months post-fracture. Our primary outcome was moderate-to-severe persistent post-surgical pain. We constructed a mixed-effects log-binomial model to explore the effect of CBT versus usual care on moderate-to-severe persistent post-surgical pain over 12 months postfracture. We randomized 1009 participants to app-based CBT (n = 506) or usual care (n = 503). The mean age of participants was 44.5 years, and 129 (12.8%) presented with an open fracture. Adherence to CBT was modest, with 237/506 patients (46.8%) completing all 7 modules. App-based CBT, compared with usual care, did not reduce the risk of persistent postsurgical pain over 12 months postfracture (30.8% v. 30.3%, adjusted relative risk 1.02, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.89 to 1.16). The 365-day probability of returning to leisure activities without restrictions was 29.0% in the intervention group and 22.4% in the control group (hazard ratio 1.33, 95% CI 1.00 to 1.77). The other secondary outcomes showed no significant differences between treatments. Among adults with an operatively managed extremity fracture, app-based CBT did not reduce the risk of persistent postsurgical pain over 12 months. Future research is warranted to develop more effective CBT approaches for adults with extremity fractures and to evaluate alternative supportive interventions that may be more acceptable to patients with fracture.
