title: Computational Modeling of Effort Allocation in First-Episode Psychosis and First-Episode Bipolar Disorder: Cognitive and Clinical Correlates.
journal: Biological psychiatry. Cognitive neuroscience and neuroimaging
abstract: Motivational deficits can be seen in bipolar disorder, as in schizophrenia. However, whether such deficits reflect a shared transdiagnostic impairment across psychotic and bipolar disorders from the early stages of illness remains unclear. This study examined effort expenditure for reward in individuals with first-episode psychosis (FEP) and first-episode bipolar disorder (FEBD), compared with healthy controls (HC). We also evaluated the relationship of these deficits in willingness to exert effort to clinical ratings and global cognition. Effort-cost decision-making (ECDM) was evaluated in the FEP (n=44), the FEBD (n=46), and HC groups (n=41) using Effort-Expenditure for Rewards Task (EEfRT). The probability × reward × group interaction was significant in the EEfRT (F = 5.12, p < .001). This study showed that participants with FEP and FEBD were less likely to choose the harder task and maximize their reward, as the probability of obtaining the reward and the reward magnitude increased. Hierarchical drift diffusion modeling further demonstrated that reward magnitude and probability influenced effort-based decisions differently in patient groups relative to controls, with more pronounced alterations in FEP. These findings suggest disrupted integration of reward-related information during effort-cost computation in the early stages of psychotic and bipolar disorders. Deficits in ECDM, while the patients were clinically stable, may indicate shared mechanisms in motivation in psychosis and bipolar disorder. The underlying mechanisms contributing to motivational abnormalities need to be clarified to create novel intervention strategies in the early stages of the disorders.

title: Reoperations After Lateral Rectus Resection/Plication Versus Medial Rectus Recession for Age-Related Distance Esotropia.
abstract: Medial rectus (MR) recession and lateral rectus (LR) resection/plication are common surgical approaches for age-related distance esotropia (ARDE), but relative advantages of the two approaches are unclear. This study evaluates their comparative efficacy, rate of reoperation, and time to reoperations. Retrospective, comparative interventional case series. Consecutive patients with ARDE undergoing strabismus surgery between 2014 and 2025 were reviewed. Surgical alignment effect and time to recurrence and reoperation. The study included 86 patients (58 females, 28 males) of mean age 70.5±8.7 years (standard deviation). Median postoperative follow-up was 1.5 (Interquartile range, IQR: 0.6-3.1, range: 0.5-10.8) years, and 61% were followed for more than 1 year. There was no difference between MR recession and LR resection/plication in the 34-37% rate of interventions by spectacle prism or reoperation required for unsatisfactory surgical outcomes. The reduction in distance ET in the LR resection/plication group was 12.6±9.8 (range: -2 to 38) Δ, similar to the 9.1±7.3 (range: -6 to 25) Δ in the MR recession group (p=0.067). Both procedures demonstrated identical surgical dose responses of 2Δ/mm. There was an insignificant trend towards higher reoperation of 30% in the MR group than 23% in the LR group. Median time to reoperation was longer at 2.8 (IQR:1.8-6.4) years after MR recession than LR resection/plication at 0.7 (IQR: 0.7-1.2) years (p=0.001). Both MR recession and LR resection/plication have similar early surgical effect and eventual rate of reoperation for recurrence of ARDE. Patients undergoing LR resection/plication require earlier reoperation.

title: Cyclodextrin-formulated ferrocifen penetrates the brain and significantly improves survival in an orthotopic mouse model of glioblastoma.
journal: European journal of pharmaceutical sciences : official journal of the European Federation for Pharmaceutical Sciences
abstract: Despite intensive chemotherapeutic and radiotherapeutic approaches for its treatment, glioblastoma (GBM) remains incurable, in part due to the difficulty of active molecules in crossing the blood-brain-barrier (BBB). Developing a suitable formulation for molecules with promising in vitro anticancer activity thus represents an essential step toward their in vivo translation. We report here the formulation of the lipophilic compound P15, a ferrocenyl analog of hydroxytamoxifen with broad antiproliferative activity, in randomly methylated β-cyclodextrin (RAMEB), together with the extensive characterization of the inclusion complex, pharmacokinetic (PK) studies, and an in vivo efficacy study in an orthotopic model of human glioblastoma in mice. Inclusion of P15 as its citrate salt is significantly more efficient, with a 5 mM solution of RAMEB being able to solubilize 12 times more P15-cit than P15. The inclusion complex P15-cit@RAMEB exhibits a favorable stability constant on the order of 104 M-1, as determined from the phase solubility diagram. The inclusion complex is characterized by a 2:1 host:guest ratio, with that the ferrocenyl moiety inserted into one of the cyclodextrins while the other incorporates an aromatic ring. PK analyses suggest a marked biodistribution of P15 in the mouse brain following IV administration of P15-cit@RAMEB at 20 mg/kg. Crucially, the survival of orthotopic GBM-bearing mice is significantly improved, resulting in 17-33% long-term survivors. RNA sequencing analysis of treated mouse brains compared with controls reveals that the treatment is associated with the inhibition of pathways related to angiogenesis, metal ion homeostasis and calcium signaling. Formulation of the citrate form of P15 in RAMEB represents a promising strategy for developing a more effective therapy for GBM patients.

title: HSPB1 in Dorsal Hippocampal Astrocytes Contributes to Stress-Induced Reinstatement of Methamphetamine Conditioned Place Preference.
abstract: Methamphetamine (MA) addiction is a chronic neuropsychiatric disorder characterized by compulsive drug-seeking behavior and a high relapse risk driven by the persistent retrieval of reward-associated memories. Although astrocytes are increasingly recognized as important modulators of drug-associated behaviors and reward memories, their contributions to MA-associated contextual memory remain incompletely understood. Here, we investigated the role of dorsal hippocampal CA1 (dCA1) astrocytes in a stress-induced reinstatement model of MA conditioned place preference (CPP) in female mice. Reinstatement of MA CPP elevated expression of astrocytic markers GFAP and S100β and enhanced Ca2+ signals in dCA1 astrocytes. Chemogenetic inhibition of dCA1 astrocytes significantly attenuated CPP reinstatement. Proteomic profiling of hippocampal tissue revealed heat shock protein beta-1 (HSPB1) as a differentially expressed protein during reinstatement. Subsequent immunohistochemical and immunofluorescence analyses revealed increased HSPB1 immunoreactivity in the dCA1 and its predominant colocalization with GFAP-positive astrocytes. Notably, pharmacological inhibition of HSPB1 using the J2 inhibitor, or GFAP-promoter-driven HSPB1 knockdown robustly suppressed stress-induced reinstatement of MA CPP. These findings reveal that HSPB1 in dCA1 astrocytes contributes to stress-induced reinstatement of MA-associated contextual preference.

title: Neuroprotective Effects of Remdesivir in ICV-STZ Induced Alzheimer-Like Pathology: Potential Involvement of ACE2-Associated Signaling.
abstract: Alzheimer's disease involves interacting metabolic, oxidative, and inflammatory disturbances, with accumulating evidence implicating dysregulation of the brain renin-angiotensin system in disease-related pathology. This study investigated the neuroprotective effects of remdesivir against intracerebroventricular streptozotocin (ICV-STZ)-induced Alzheimer-like pathology and examined the potential involvement of ACE1/ACE2-associated signaling. Following ICV-STZ administration on Days 1 and 3, remdesivir treatment was initiated on Day 4 and continued once daily through Day 31. Remdesivir was evaluated using molecular docking, molecular dynamics simulation, behavioral testing, cholinesterase inhibition assays, biochemical analyses, ELISA, immunohistochemistry, qRT-PCR, Western blotting, and histopathology. ICV-STZ induced memory-related and affective-like behavioral impairments, altered exploratory activity, reduced ACE2 expression, increased ACE1 expression, oxidative stress, NLRP3/NF-κB-associated neuroinflammation, amyloid/tau-related alterations, and neuronal degeneration. Remdesivir dose-dependently improved behavioral and biochemical outcomes, increased ACE2 expression, reduced ACE1 expression, and attenuated neuroinflammation, oxidative injury, and neurodegeneration, with the most pronounced effects observed at 30 mg/kg. Pharmacological modulation with DX600 and diminazene aceturate altered the protective effects of remdesivir, providing supportive but not definitive evidence for the involvement of ACE2-associated signaling. However, ACE2 enzymatic activity and downstream Ang-(1-7)/Mas receptor signaling were not directly assessed. Remdesivir also inhibited AChE and BChE, with IC50 values of 237.4 μM and 535.7 μM, respectively. These findings demonstrate that early remdesivir intervention attenuates the development of ICV-STZ-induced Alzheimer-like pathology and suggest that modulation of the ACE1/ACE2 expression balance may be associated with its antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and neuroprotective effects.

title: Miro1 and mitochondrial dysfunction in Huntington's disease: Emerging mechanistic links and therapeutic perspectives.
abstract: Huntington's disease (HD) is a chronic, hereditary, and ultimately fatal neurological disorder that is transmitted in an autosomal dominant manner through an abnormal expansion of trinucleotide CAG repeats in the huntingtin gene, which encodes a mutant protein with an expanded polyglutamine tract. HD occurs in approximately 5-10 individuals per 100,000 people worldwide, and is associated with increasing motor dysfunction, cognitive decline and profound neuropsychiatric disorder with a selective vulnerability of the striatal medium spiny neurons. Early and integral to HD pathogenesis is mitochondrial dysfunction, before the onset of clinical symptoms and obvious neurodegeneration. In the context of mitochondrial regulation, the atypical Rho GTPase Miro1 has emerged as a key regulator that integrates mitochondrial motility, calcium sensing, fusion/fission dynamics, and mitophagy. Mutant huntingtin interferes with the assembly of motor-adaptor complexes containing Miro1, mitochondrial transport along axons, the regulation of motility arrest by Ca2+-sensing mechanisms, and the degradation of Miro1 by PINK1/Parkin, leading to impaired mitochondrial quality control and propagation of bioenergetic stress. These converging abnormalities are linked to molecular pathology characterised by mitochondrial mislocalization, insufficient mitochondrial turnover and synaptic failure resulting in selective degeneration of HD neurons. A study using zQ175 HD model mice demonstrated that Miro1overexpression partially rescued impaired anterograde mitochondrial transport in striatal neurons. However, this gain-of-function rescue does not establish endogenous Miro1 deficiency or demonstrate that Miro1 dysfunction is a primary driver of HD pathology. This review critically analyses the molecular mechanisms underlying mitochondrial dysfunction in HD, particularly Miro1, its implications for HD neurodegeneration, and its therapeutic potential.

title: Urolithin A plus EGCG enhances mitophagy associated pathways, mitochondrial dynamics, and bioenergetic function in humanized amyloid-β knock-in mice.
abstract: Mitochondrial dysfunction and impaired mitochondrial quality control are increasingly recognized as important contributors to Alzheimer's disease (AD). Urolithin A is a mitophagy-promoting metabolite, whereas epigallocatechin-3-gallate (EGCG) has antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and anti-amyloidogenic properties. In the present study, we evaluated the effects of urolithin A alone and in combination with EGCG on mitochondrial homeostasis in humanized amyloid-β knock-in (hAbKI) mice. Three-month-old hAbKI mice were treated with urolithin A (2.5 mg/kg) or urolithin A plus EGCG (25 mg/kg) by intraperitoneal injection three times per week for four months. At seven months of age, mitochondrial dynamics, mitochondrial biogenesis, mitophagy/autophagy-associated pathways, mitochondrial ultrastructure, ATP production, oxidative stress, synaptic and dendritic markers, glial and neuronal proteins, soluble Aβ40 and Aβ42 levels, and behavioral performance were evaluated. Quantitative reverse transcriptase polymerase chain reaction (qRT-PCR) analysis showed reduced expression of the mitochondrial fission genes Drp1 and Fis1 and increased expression of the fusion genes Mfn1, Mfn2, and Opa1 following treatment. Mitochondrial biogenesis-associated genes, including PGC1α, Nrf1 and TFAM, were also increased. These transcriptional changes were supported by immunoblotting analyses. Treatment further increased mitophagy- and autophagy-associated markers, including PINK1, Parkin, ATG5, LC3B, Beclin1, and BCL2. Transmission electron microscopy demonstrated increased mitochondrial length, reduced mitochondrial fragmentation. These changes were accompanied by increased mitochondrial ATP levels and reduced hydrogen peroxide and 4-hydroxynonenal levels. Both treatment regimens were also associated with increased synaptic and dendritic measures, reduced Iba1 and GFAP expression, increased NeuN levels, lower soluble Aβ40 and Aβ42 concentrations, and improved performance in several behavioral tasks. Across multiple mitochondrial and neuronal endpoints, the magnitude of the response was greater following combined urolithin A and EGCG treatment. These findings indicate that urolithin A modulates multiple components of mitochondrial quality control in hAbKI mice and that co-treatment with EGCG is associated with broader improvements in mitochondrial and neuronal homeostasis. Further studies are required to define the specific contribution of EGCG and to directly assess mitophagic flux and mitochondrial respiration.

title: Pro-inflammatory infiltrating T cells promote persistent microglial activation and neuronal loss following SAH.
abstract: Aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH) initiates a robust neuroinflammatory response, yet the specific contribution of T cells to injury evolution remains poorly understood. Here, we demonstrate that T cell infiltration into the brain parenchyma critically modulates microglial activation and promotes neuronal loss after experimental SAH. Using a murine pre-chiasmatic injection model of SAH, we demonstrate the emergence of neurological deficits accompanied by cerebral edema, vasospasm, glial activation, and neuronal loss up to 7-days post injury (dpi). Targeted transcriptomic profiling revealed a sustained neuroimmune response at 7-dpi characterized by a major involvement of T cells and microglia activation. Immunohistochemistry revealed infiltrating CD3+ T cell clusters in the brain parenchyma of SAH mice. Flow cytometry analysis confirmed that SAH induces adaptive T cell-specific infiltration and further identified a pro-inflammatory CD4+/IFN-γ and γδ+/IL-17 response. In a longitudinal human SAH cohort, rising CSF neurofilament light chain (NfL) and IL-6 levels were paralleled by selective enrichment of CD4+ T cells in the CSF, with increased Ki67, IL-17, and IFN-γ, consistent with an activated pro-inflammatory effector CD4+ T cell phenotype. In mice, T cell presence spatially correlated with regions of microglial reactivity and neuronal loss. Notably, CD3 knockout mice exhibited reduced microglial activation and reduced hippocampal neuronal degeneration and greater preservation of NeuN immunoreactivity compared with wild-type controls. These findings identify T cells as key amplifiers of post-SAH neuroinflammatory response and support their contribution to microglial reactivity and neuronal injury after SAH. Targeting T cell-microglia crosstalk represents a novel therapeutic avenue for mitigating secondary brain injury after SAH.

title: Asynchronous neurovascular and glial responses after particulate air pollution exposure declines.
abstract: Particulate air pollution can decline after emission control or filtration, yet the subsequent course of neurovascular and glial abnormalities remains uncertain. This critical narrative review examines experimental post-exposure reports and human exposure-reduction studies, distinguishing cellular state, direct function, and mechanistic attribution. Experimental findings show different temporal patterns across endothelial inflammatory markers, microglial states, brain metabolism, and behavior. Early blood-brain barrier (BBB) leakage is documented after diesel exhaust, but later normalization of the same function is not established. Some inflammatory measures attenuate after a switch to filtered air, whereas other abnormalities remain detectable weeks or months later. A single late measurement demonstrates an abnormality at that interval rather than its uninterrupted persistence. Human studies report both favorable and null cognitive or developmental outcomes after reduced exposure; these outcomes do not identify cell-specific recovery. Particle composition, exposure route, age, sex, and sampling schedule limit comparison across models. The evidence supports asynchronous post-exposure responses rather than a common sequence of functional restoration. Recovery of a specified neurovascular or glial task requires a documented abnormal phase followed by repeated measurement of that task, while attribution requires separate evaluation of continuing peripheral input.

title: "Rotations in Other Specialties During Neurosurgical Training in Africa: A Multi-country Cross-Sectional Study".
abstract: Rotations in specialties outside neurosurgery contribute to the development of multidisciplinary competencies during neurosurgical training. However, the experiences and perceptions of African neurosurgical trainees and specialists regarding these rotations remain insufficiently documented. To describe respondents' self-reported experiences and perceptions regarding the type, timing, duration, and educational value of rotations in other specialties during neurosurgical training. A multicounty, descriptive cross-sectional electronic survey recruited neurosurgery residents and qualified neurosurgeons trained in Africa through professional networks using non-probability convenience sampling from April 30 to August 30, 2026. A structured questionnaire, pilot-tested among 10 senior neurosurgeons trained outside Africa and excluded from the study, assessed specialty rotations, international training exposure, perceived educational benefits, and curricular gaps. Quantitative data were summarized using descriptive statistics, while free-text responses were descriptively categorized by one investigator and summarized using frequencies and percentages. 97 participants from 19 African countries were included, comprising 49 residents (50.5%) and 48 qualified neurosurgeons (49.5%). Overall, 86 (88.7%) had undertaken rotations outside neurosurgery. The most frequently reported rotations were General surgery (n=67) and neurology (n=62). Rotations were most reported during the first three years of training. 36 participants (37.1%) reported international rotations. Among surveyed African neurosurgery residents and qualified neurosurgeons, rotations in other specialties were commonly reported and generally perceived as educationally valuable. These findings may inform future discussions and the development of competency-based neurosurgical training curricula adapted to different African contexts but should not be interpreted as representative of all African training programs.

title: Amyloid-β dimers bind to microglial TLR2 to induce early neuroinflammation and cognitive deficits in Alzheimer's disease.
abstract: Previous studies have shown that amyloid-β (Aβ) oligomers are implicated in the pathogenesis of Alzheimer's disease (AD). Aβ oligomers include various molecules with distinct characteristics, such as dimers and trimers; among these, Aβ dimers have been found to possess neurotoxicity. This study found that Aβ dimers can induce microglial proliferation, enhanced phagocytosis, and pro-inflammatory polarization in the mouse brain even before cognitive impairment occurs, and this effect was validated in vitro using BV2 cells. Mechanistically, Aβ dimers bind to the microglial receptor TLR2, activating the downstream NF-κB signaling pathway and upregulating the expression of inflammatory factors. Knocking down TLR2 significantly reverses the Aβ dimer-induced inflammatory response and alleviates microglial-mediated neuronal damage. Furthermore, repeated intracerebral injections of Aβ dimers lead to impaired learning and memory in mice, as well as loss of hippocampal neurons and synapses; these changes are independent of amyloid plaque deposition and tau protein hyperphosphorylation. In summary, Aβ dimers induce early neuroinflammation and cognitive deficits by binding to TLR2 on microglia, providing a new molecular target for early intervention in AD.

title: Association of metoprolol with temporal changes in SIRT1, oxidative stress, and inflammatory biomarkers.
abstract: There is a paucity of studies on the effect of beta-blocker on sirtuins (SIRT1)-mediated inflammation and oxidative stress in ischemic stroke. We report the effect of metoprolol on the temporal kinetics of SIRT1-mediated oxidative stress markers [catalase (CAT), glutathione peroxidase (GPx), malondialdehyde (MDA), and reactive oxygen species (ROS)], proinflammatory cytokines (TNFα and IL1β), and their association with outcomes. This was a sub-analysis of our earlier study on effect of beta-blocker in acute stroke. Forty-eight patients within 3-days of ischemic stroke were included. Their demographic characteristics, risk factors for stroke, GCS/NIHSS score, hematological and biochemical parameters, electrocardiogram, echocardiography, and cranial-MRI findings were noted. SIRT1, TNFα, and IL1β mRNA fold-changes were measured by using real-time PCR, and GPx, CAT, MDA, and ROS were measured by using a spectrophotometer. These biomarkers were also measured in 59 healthy-controls. The outcome was defined at 1 and 3-months using the modified Rankin Scale. Twenty-eight patients received metoprolol, and 20 received amlodipine. There is a gradual reduction in TNFα, IL1β, ROS, and MDA and an increase in CAT level in both groups; however, more marked in the metoprolol group. On day 15, the metoprolol group had a comparable level of SIRT1, TNFα, IL1β, and CAT to those with the healthy controls. Metoprolol in acute ischemic stroke helps in upregulating SIRT1 and CAT and downregulating TNFα and IL1β; however, the overall p-value for treatment-by-time interaction was insignificant. The patients in the metoprolol group had a better outcome at 3-months. A large study is needed to confirm these findings.

title: A single post-stress dose of caffeine preserves threat-safety discrimination but not fear extinction in rats exposed to single prolonged stress.
abstract: Post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) is characterized by impaired fear extinction and fear overgeneralization, yet no early pharmacological intervention has been established. Because the pathophysiology of PTSD develops over a modifiable period after trauma, we tested whether a single moderate dose of caffeine (30mg/kg) administered immediately after single prolonged stress (SPS) protects fear regulation and its underlying neurochemistry in male rats. The abilities of threat-safety discrimination and fear extinction were assessed using a Pavlovian discriminative fear conditioning paradigm, and tissue levels of serotonin (5-HT), dopamine (DA), norepinephrine (NE), and neuropeptide Y (NPY) were quantified in the hippocampus, medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC), and amygdala. The results demonstrated that caffeine produced a behavioral dissociation: it restored threat-safety discrimination but did not rescue the extinction retention deficits. This selectivity was mirrored neurochemically. Caffeine restored SPS-induced reductions in hippocampal 5-HT and DA and in mPFC NPY, but did not restore hippocampal NE or mPFC monoamines, and no changes were detected in the amygdala. These findings suggest that a single post-stress dose of caffeine acts through region-specific neurochemical pathways rather than providing global protection. Therefore, caffeine emerges as a promising and accessible candidate for early post-stress intervention targeting fear overgeneralization.

title: Transcriptional dynamics of glutamate excitotoxicity in the mammalian cochlea.
abstract: Hearing loss affects approximately 1.3 billion people worldwide and is frequently accompanied by tinnitus, hyperacusis, and difficulty hearing in noise. Some of these symptoms may be linked to cochlear synaptopathy, the loss of synaptic connections between inner hair cells and spiral ganglion neurons. Glutamate excitotoxicity is a key driver of synaptic injury, and the molecular programs governing cochlear synapse vulnerability and repair are under active investigation. Here, we integrated neonatal cochlear explant models, adult noise-exposure models, and single-cell and spatially resolved transcriptomics to identify convergent and divergent patterns in transcriptional responses of AMPA-type glutamate receptor subunits and neurotrophin receptor signaling in acute response to excitotoxic injury across multiple contexts. In neonatal CD1 mouse cochlear explants, excitotoxic injury and subsequent neurotrophin-3 exposure activated a repair-permissive transcriptional program characterized by increased expression of AMPA receptor subunits (Gria2, Gria3, Gria4) and the neurotrophin receptor Ntrk3, predominantly within a spiral ganglion neuron population expressing Type 1C-like markers. In contrast, adult CBA/CaJ mice exposed to noise induced a coordinated downregulation of AMPA receptor subunits (Gria2, Gria4) and Ntrk3, primarily in Type 1A neuronal subtypes. Spatial RNA in situ hybridization further revealed that this downregulation is tonotopically restricted, with selective loss of Gria2 and Ntrk3 in high-frequency regions that sustain the greatest synaptic degeneration. Together, these findings reveal opposing, context-dependent molecular responses to excitotoxic injury, and may suggest that synaptic regeneration in the adult cochlea could be enhanced by reactivation of a neonatal-like transcriptional program to increase neurotrophin receptor availability for synapse recovery after noise-induced damage.

title: Linking ferroptosis to chronic sleep deprivation: emerging insights into mechanisms and interventions.
abstract: Sleep is essential for maintaining systemic homeostasis, facilitating tissue repair, and consolidating neural circuitry. In modern society, however, accelerated lifestyles and rising work pressures have made sleep deprivation (SD) a pressing public health concern. Recent studies increasingly link chronic sleep deprivation (CSD) to various neurological disorders. The precise mechanisms, however, are not fully understood. Notably, ferroptosis as a regulated form of cell death has emerged as a potential link between CSD and neurodegeneration. This narrative review critically synthesizes evidence linking CSD with ferroptosis, with particular emphasis on iron handling, lipid peroxidation, the system Xc - -GSH-GPX4 defense axis, mitochondrial/redox stress, and neuroinflammatory signaling. Furthermore, previous studies suggest that interventions such as ketogenic diets, ω-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids, vitamin B6 and phytochemicals supplementation can modulate ferroptosis in CSD mouse model. Therefore, they may serve as potential nutritional and pharmacological therapeutic targets. However, current evidence remains predominantly preclinical, and many studies rely on ferroptosis-associated biomarkers rather than definitive causal tests. A deeper understanding of the mechanistic interplay between ferroptosis and CSD will not only advance our comprehension of CSD-induced neural impairment, but also provide a theoretical basis for the development of novel therapeutic strategies for sleep-related disorders.

title: Machine Learning-Driven Prediction of Neurochemical Signatures in the Rett Syndrome Mouse Brain.
abstract: Rett syndrome is a genetic neurodevelopmental disorder caused by mutations of the MECP2 gene. It is characterized by severe neurological, cognitive, autonomic, and motor dysfunctions. Central catecholaminergic deficits, together with alterations in GABAergic and glutamatergic systems, have previously been identified in the brain of Mecp2 knockout mice using conventional data analyses. Here, we reanalyzed neurochemical data from this well-established mouse model using machine-learning approaches to identify new neurochemical information. We leveraged a neurochemical database featuring tissue concentrations of dopamine, noradrenaline, serotonin, GABA and glutamate from micro-dissected brain areas in both Mecp2-knockout and wild-type mice. We then extracted qualitative and quantitative data at the early-onset and fully symptomatic stages of the disease. Five machine learning models were trained to predict genotype, and their predictive performance was evaluated. Despite the small number of individuals per group, the best model was obtained with XGBoost fitting. SHAP-derived variables of importance analysis identified neurotransmitters and brain regions that were consistent with neurochemical alterations previously implicated in the pathophysiology of Rett syndrome. Our results indicate that machine learning, which remains largely underused in the field of neurochemistry, can effectively predict group differences from brain neurochemical profiles in a well-established mouse model for Rett syndrome. The satisfying performances highlight the potential of machine learning and modern computational tools to extract additional information from existing neurochemical datasets, complement conventional analyses, and for the redesign of future neurochemical studies.

title: Development and Validation of a Neonatal Mouse Brain Stereotaxic Injection Platform for Maintaining Perioperative Physiological Homeostasis.
abstract: Neonatal mouse brain stereotaxic injection is an essential experimental technique for investigating neurodevelopmental regulation and neonatal neurological disorders. However, immature thermoregulation and limited anesthetic tolerance make neonatal mice highly susceptible to uncontrolled perioperative hypothermia and physiological instability, which compromise postoperative survival, increase experimental variability, and may confound disease modeling and the interpretation of intervention outcomes. We developed an integrated digital temperature-controlled stereotaxic platform that combines non-invasive head fixation, inhalation anesthesia, and real-time closed-loop thermal regulation. The platform provides continuous perioperative thermal support to maintain physiological homeostasis and is compatible with a wide range of neonatal intracerebral injection applications. The platform maintained stable perioperative body temperature, significantly improved postoperative survival, and reliably supported secondary intracerebral intervention after brain injury, ultra-early gene knockout, and microglial viral tracing in neonatal mice. Existing neonatal stereotaxic procedures rely on hypothermia-induced anesthesia, room-temperature surgery, or external warming methods such as warm-water systems and heating pads, which may provide insufficiently stable temperature control and require additional operational steps. In contrast, the present platform integrates stereotaxic injection and active temperature regulation, simplifying surgical procedures while enabling precise thermal management and maintaining intraoperative body temperature in neonatal mice. By integrating physiological support with stereotaxic surgery, this platform provides a standardized, reliable, and reproducible approach for neonatal mouse intracerebral injection and facilitates advanced experimental manipulation in neonatal neuroscience research and disease modeling.

title: Neural Connectome Mapping of Chronotype in Young Adults: Associations with Neurotransmitter Profiles and Longitudinal Self-Control.
abstract: Chronotype is associated with self-regulation, but its functional connectivity correlates, neurotransmitter correspondence, and longitudinal associations with self-control remain unclear. We applied connectome-based predictive modeling (CPM) in a longitudinal cohort to identify resting-state connectivity features associated with chronotype. Cross-validated predictions showed a small correlation with reduced Morningness-Eveningness Questionnaire (rMEQ) scores in the discovery set (n = 816, r = 0.118, pperm = 0.007). A similar association was observed in validation set 1, a baseline hold-out sample from the same cohort (n = 681, r = 0.125, pperm < 0.001). Longitudinal evaluation used validation set 2, comprising two-year follow-up data from a subset of participants in validation set 1 (n = 594, r = 0.134, pperm < 0.001), providing a within-cohort assessment of whether the association was stable over time. Node-importance maps showed spatial correspondence with neurotransmitter maps. Both connectivity sets shared GABA-A and VAChT associations, with relatively receptor-weighted and transporter-weighted profiles in the positive and negative sets, respectively. In participants with complete two-wave data (n = 563), cross-lagged panel models indicated that baseline self-control was prospectively associated with higher positive-set strength (β = 0.256, p < 0.001) and lower negative-set strength (β = -0.228, p < 0.001); reverse paths were not significant. These findings provide evidence for chronotype-related functional connectivity features and their associations with neurotransmitter distributions and self-control in young adults. The validation and longitudinal evidence is limited to a single-site cohort, and cross-cohort generalizability remains to be established.

title: Spontaneously emerging patterns show category-biased similarity to task-evoked visual patterns beyond human visual cortex.
abstract: In the absence of any task, spontaneous brain activity exhibits patterns that resemble those evoked by natural stimuli and behaviors. This raises the possibility that resting-state activity patterns may relate to maintenance and consolidation of behaviorally relevant information states. Using functional MRI (fMRI) data from 100 healthy adults in the Human Connectome Project, we investigated whether neural signals evoked by specific visual stimuli (body parts, faces, places, tools) show similarity to resting-state activity across non-canonical visual areas, i.e., motor and association cortices. Participants underwent a working memory task and resting-state scanning. We analyzed multivoxel pattern similarity between task-evoked activations and spontaneous activity in bilateral hand motor regions and attention-related networks. Spatial correlations between task-evoked multivoxel patterns for each visual category and frame-by-frame resting-state signals were computed, with the upper 90% distribution percentile (U90) as a similarity metric. We found that resting-state patterns in the left hemisphere hand motor region showed significantly higher similarity to tool-evoked patterns than place-evoked patterns, consistent with the interpretation that tools recruit motor affordances and hand‑object associations in motor cortex. In the bilateral dorsal attention network, resting-task similarity for non-face evoked patterns significantly exceeded that for faces. Moreover, effects localized to posterior dorsal attention network, aligning with the dorsal visual pathway's role in spatial-action coding of behaviorally relevant objects. These results suggest that resting-state activity in non-visual cortices shows category-biased similarity to task-evoked visual patterns, consistent with the view that spontaneous neural dynamics preferentially reactivate ecologically salient stimuli.

title: Advances in Retinal Cellular Imaging: Towards Single-Cell Resolution and Functional Biomarkers.
journal: Progress in retinal and eye research
abstract: Retinal imaging has traditionally described tissue and layer level pathology, whereas direct assessment of individual cells in the living human retina has been limited by ocular aberrations, optical contrast and image analysis constraints. Adaptive optics (AO) has substantially changed this landscape by improving lateral resolution and enabling in vivo visualization of photoreceptors, retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), ganglion-cell-layer structures, immune cells and microvasculature. This review discusses human retinal cellular imaging across three major AO-enhanced platforms: flood-illumination adaptive optics (FIAO), adaptive optics optical coherence tomography (AO-OCT) and adaptive optics scanning laser ophthalmoscopy (AOSLO). These modalities provide complementary capabilities, including rapid en face imaging, depth-resolved volumetric assessment and flexible confocal, non-confocal and fluorescence-based contrast. Recent progress is also being shaped by faster wavefront correction, wider-field acquisition, compressed multichannel imaging, sensorless AO and artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted reconstruction, segmentation and quantification. Beyond optical resolution, molecular labeling strategies are beginning to add biological specificity to retinal cellular imaging. Indocyanine green (ICG) supports AO-assisted assessment of RPE mosaic contrast, annexin V-based Detection of Apoptosing Retinal Cells (DARC) provides a molecular readout of retinal cell stress and apoptosis, and curcumin-based imaging has been explored as an experimental retinal amyloid marker in Alzheimer's disease. Together, these advances indicate a shift from high-resolution visualization alone towards cellular and molecular biomarkers of disease activity, progression and treatment response. Further translation will require standardized acquisition, robust automated analysis, multimodal validation and larger prospective studies across devices, disease populations and clinical sites.

title: Neurochemical signatures of morphometric network reorganization in Duchenne muscular dystrophy: Links to cognition and behavior.
abstract: Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) is associated with neurocognitive behavior problems and regional morphometric abnormalities, yet large-scale brain network reorganization and its molecular correlations remain unclear. Here, we explored whether remodeling of the individual-level morphological similarity network (MSN) in DMD aligns with specific neurotransmitter systems and associates with cognitive, behavioral, and motor performance. We studied 111 boys with DMD and 80 age- and sex-matched healthy controls (HCs). Individual MSNs were derived from T1-weighted MRI. Global and nodal graph-theoretical metrics were compared between groups, and network-based statistics (NBS) were used to identify altered subnetworks. Spatial correlations linked altered MSN maps to normative PET/SPECT neurotransmitter maps, and Spearman correlations related MSN alterations and neurochemical indices to clinical measures. The global small-world organization of MSNs was preserved. However, boys with DMD showed increased degree centrality (DC) in the bilateral hippocampus and left cerebellar lobule 3, and decreased DC in the right cerebellar lobule 7b. NBS identified a cerebellar-frontotemporal-subcortical morphological circuit characterized by reduced morphological similarity. MSN alterations showed significant spatial associations with dopaminergic, serotonergic, GABAergic, glutamatergic, cholinergic, and endocannabinoid systems, and the strength of these associations and network disruption were associated with poorer cognitive, motor, and behavioral performance. Children with DMD exhibit MSN remodeling centered on a cerebellar-frontotemporal-subcortical morphological circuit that is neurochemically coupled to specific neurotransmitter systems and linked to cognitive, behavioral, and motor deficits. This study elucidates potential neurochemical mechanisms underlying neurobehavioral abnormalities in DMD and may provide biological insights to inform the development of neuromodulation-based therapeutic strategies.

title: Examining the longitudinal effects of maternal physical discipline on children's systemic low-grade inflammation across childhood.
abstract: Maternal physical discipline remains a common child-rearing practice worldwide. Although its harmful effects on children's socioemotional development are well documented, less is known about how these experiences become biologically embedded and whether they are reflected in chronic low-grade inflammation as a marker of mental and physical health. The present study prospectively examined the association between the frequency of maternal physical discipline and subsequent changes in children's systemic low-grade inflammation across middle childhood. Longitudinal data were drawn from 353 mother-child dyads enrolled in the multi-ethnic Singaporean GUSTO birth cohort. Mothers reported their use of physical discipline when children were 6 years old. Children's systemic inflammation was indexed by repeated blood serum C-reactive protein assessments at ages 6, 8, 10 and 12 years. Analyses were pre-registered and conducted using cumulative link mixed-effects modelling, while adjusting for a range of sociodemographic and health-related covariates. Children's C-reactive protein levels declined across ages 6 to 12 years. Importantly, higher levels of physical discipline predicted less decline in C-reactive protein over time (b = 0.09, SE = 0.04, t = 2.46, 95 % CI [0.02, 0.16], p = 0.01), as well as relatively higher levels of C-reactive protein at age 12 years. Findings indicate that more exposure to physical discipline may impact the trajectory of children's inflammation levels across childhood, suggesting a physiological cost of this disciplinary practice. These results reinforce the importance of reducing the use of physical discipline to support healthier developmental trajectories.

title: Elevation-associated variation in bumble bee venom composition is not retained under common-garden conditions.
abstract: Bumble bees (Bombus) are vital pollinators across diverse habitats. Female bumble bees have a defensive, venomous sting used against predators. Little is known about the factors associated with intraspecific variation in bumble bee venom. We studied the venom composition of wild-caught Bombus vosnesenskii and tested for elevation-associated differences along an elevation gradient in Oregon, USA. Using a common garden approach with laboratory-reared colonies sourced from wild populations, we also tested the influence of captivity on venom response. Proteomic analysis using liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry revealed clear elevation-associated variation in venom composition among wild populations, particularly in the abundance of the bombolitin-like antimicrobial peptide. By contrast, comparable elevation-associated differences were not evident under common-garden conditions when colonies were reared under shared laboratory conditions. More broadly, our findings demonstrate substantial intraspecific variation in bumble bee venom composition, and captive populations may not fully reflect wild variability, impacting the interpretation of venom studies relying on captive species.

title: Dialogical therapy plus treatment as usual versus treatment as usual in adults with distressing and persistent auditory hallucinations in the UK (Talking with Voices-II): a randomised controlled trial.
abstract: Existing treatments for auditory hallucinations (hereafter voice hearing) among people with serious mental health problems (SMHPs; diagnoses include schizophrenia spectrum disorders, bipolar disorders, and personality disorders) show only modest clinical benefits, produce inconsistent long-term outcomes, and seldom prioritise personal recovery as a primary treatment goal. We aimed to investigate the effectiveness of Talking with Voices (TwV), a lived-experience informed intervention in which therapists engage in direct dialogue with voices, in improving both personal recovery and clinical outcomes for individuals experiencing persistent and distressing voice hearing. Talking with Voices-II was a rater-blinded, parallel-arm, multisite, randomised controlled trial to test the efficacy and underlying mechanisms of TwV therapy compared with treatment as usual (TAU) in community-based National Health Service mental health services across four UK sites. Participants with SMHPs who experienced distressing voices were randomly assigned (1:1), using random-sized blocks, stratified by site and presence of schizophrenia diagnosis, to receive either TwV plus TAU or TAU alone. Therapy was provided in up to 26 sessions over 8 months, and assessments were conducted at baseline, 8 months, and 14 months by assessors masked to treatment allocation. The primary outcome was the Questionnaire about the Process of Recovery score at 8 months, a self-reported measure of personal recovery in psychosis. Secondary outcomes were voice-related measures, self-beliefs, dissociation, and post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) symptoms. The primary analysis followed the intention-to-treat principle, and moderation and mediation were prespecified in the statistical analysis plan. The mediation analysis was carried out using the mediate command, utilising bootstrapping to obtain percentile CIs. The trial was prospectively registered with ISRCTN, ISRCTN15897915, and all research and clinical procedures were co-led by individuals with lived experience of psychosis. Between Sept 1, 2023, and June 30, 2025, we screened 1316 participants, of whom 309 consented, completed baseline assessments, and were randomly assigned to either TwV plus TAU (n=156) or TAU alone (n=153). The mean age of participants was 41·1 years (SD 13·1). 159 (52%) participants were men, 145 (47%) were women, and four (1%) were another gender, and one preferred not to say; 222 (72%) participants were White. At 8 months, personal recovery was significantly better in the TwV group than in the TAU group (adjusted difference 6·97 [95% CI 5·00-8·95]; p<0·0001; standardised effect size [SES] 0·63). Significant differences favouring TwV were found for 12 (80%) of 15 of secondary outcomes, unadjusted for multiple testing, including all voice-related measures, negative self-beliefs, and PTSD outcomes, with SES ranging from 0·18 to 0·86. There were no effects on dissociation-related measures or positive self-beliefs (SES ranging from <0·01 to 0·16). An effect was still evident on personal recovery at 14 months, although reduced (adjusted difference 3·55 [0·96-6·14]; p=0·0073; SES=0·32). 55 serious adverse events occurred in 36 participants in the TwV group, and 60 serious adverse events occurred in 45 participants in the TAU group, none of which were deemed definitely related to the therapy or research procedures. TwV significantly improves personal recovery, showing efficacy for individuals with SMHPs who experience distressing voices. Further research comparing TwV with an active control and evaluating its implementation in routine care settings is warranted. National Institute for Health and Care Research.

title: Comparative efficacy and acceptability of antidepressants in the long-term treatment of major depressive disorder: a systematic review and network meta-analysis.
abstract: Major depressive disorder carries high risks of relapse and chronicity, necessitating treatments that achieve and maintain response (sustained response). This study aimed to compare antidepressants on their ability to achieve sustained response, and on acceptability, by synthesising data from randomised controlled trials. For this systematic review and network meta-analysis, we searched the Cochrane Register, AMED, CINAHL, Embase, LILACS, MEDLINE, MEDLINE In-Progress, PsycINFO, the UK National Research Register, and regulatory agency websites from inception to March 27, 2026. We included double-blind randomised controlled trials that compared any of 21 antidepressants head-to-head or with placebo for long-term treatment (>12 weeks) of adult unipolar major depressive disorder. We included enrichment, non-enrichment, continuation, and continuation-extension designs, and extracted study-level data. We could not derive the sex or gender distribution of participants other than female and did not extract data on race or ethnicity. Primary outcomes were efficacy (sustained response rate) and acceptability (all-cause discontinuation). We synthesised data in random-effects pairwise and network meta-analyses to estimate pooled odds ratios (ORs), using fluoxetine as a reference in the ranked forest plots. The primary analysis included head-to-head continuation and continuation-extension design studies. Enrichment design studies were incorporated in the analysis using a chain-of-evidence approach. Risk-of-bias assessment was done using the Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 tool. No people with lived experience were involved in the design, conduct, or interpretation of this study. From 54 231 records, 115 studies (30 428 participants; mean age 45·3 years [SD 8·5], 20 066 [66%] female) were included. In head-to-head continuation and continuation-extension design studies (35 studies; n=9888), sustained response differed across antidepressants. Escitalopram (OR 1·62, 95% CI 1·21-2·18), duloxetine (OR 1·57, 1·08-2·26), and agomelatine (OR 1·40, 1·06-1·85) showed higher sustained response rates than fluoxetine. Bupropion and reboxetine showed lower sustained response rates against four other antidepressants in the league table of pairwise comparisons. Escitalopram (OR 0·60, 0·43-0·83) and duloxetine (OR 0·64, 0·44-0·95) demonstrated lower all-cause discontinuation compared with fluoxetine, while reboxetine and milnacipran showed higher all-cause discontinuation against six and four other antidepressants, respectively, in the league table of pairwise comparisons. Sensitivity analyses incorporating enrichment-design studies corroborated these results. However, the certainty of evidence of the network meta-analysis results and the risk of bias in the included studies (19 [54%] of 35 had high risk of bias) might limit the reliability of the current findings. Antidepressants can differ in their efficacy for achieving sustained response and in their acceptability. These findings can inform the shared decision making for patients, prescribers, and carers in real-world practice. However, more head-to-head comparative studies are needed to provide reliable information about long-term effects of all licensed antidepressants. None.

title: Comparison of physiological responses and experiences between sitting semi-recumbent in bed and sitting in a chair - A randomised, crossover clinical trial.
abstract: ObjectiveEarly mobilisation of patients in intensive care is considered feasible and beneficial. However, the safety and effects of different mobilisation interventions require further research. Therefore, this study aimed to investigate and compare patient experiences and physiological responses between sitting semi-recumbent in bed and sitting in a chair.MethodsA pragmatic, randomised, clinical crossover trial was conducted as a single-day intervention. Forty-seven consecutively included patients (men/women: 34/13; mean age (SD): 70.4 (12.5)) in intensive care were randomised to begin the intervention either sitting semi-recumbent in bed or in a chair. Each treatment period lasted 40 minutes, with a minimum washout period of two hours between sessions. The haemodynamic and respiratory variables used to assess mobilisation readiness or suspension, were collected, as well as self-rated variables of pain, exertion and satisfaction.ResultsPhysiological responses to sitting were comparable between the two positions. Estimated treatment effects were small for both primary outcomes (mean arterial pressure: 0.7 mmHg, 95% CI -5.5 to 6.9, p = 0.822; PaO2/FiO2: -3.3, 95% CI -51.2 to 44.6, p = 0.890), with the confidence intervals suggesting no clinically meaningful differences between the interventions. Oxygen saturation tended to be lower in the semi-recumbent position. The self-rated variables indicated that pain increased (p=0.028) and satisfaction decreased (p=0.044) in the semi-recumbent position, while exertion was non-significant in both positions (bed: p=0.169; chair: p=0.913). No adverse events were noted.ConclusionSitting in a chair was safe and exerted similar physiological demands on the patient as the semi-recumbent position in bed. However, in the semi-recumbent position, pain increased over time, satisfaction decreased, and a trend toward decreased saturation was also observed. The findings support considering mobilisation to a chair when clinically appropriate, while taking precautions to avoid falls and other adverse events.

title: Geographic disparities and aging-related burden in reperfusion service output for acute ischemic stroke in China: A national sample spatial analysis.
abstract: Despite expanding stroke centers, regional disparities and population aging challenge acute ischemic stroke (AIS) care in China. We aimed to map the spatial distribution of AIS reperfusion therapy and identify aging-related service mismatch. This cross-sectional study analyzed hospital-level data from 2,522 mainland Chinese hospitals participating in the Survey of National Stroke Telemedicine Treatment Project. Spatial analysis was used to assess service output distribution. Multilevel mixed-effects logistic regression evaluated factors associated with treatment efficiency. A four-quadrant matrix compared regional aging rates with observed thrombolysis volume to identify high-aging-burden, low-service-output mismatch. Thrombolysis output showed an east-to-west gradient that became more pronounced after adjusting for aging population. Compared with secondary and below hospitals, tertiary hospitals had a higher monthly thrombolysis volume (10 [5-16] versus 4 [2-8]) and shorter door-to-needle time (DNT) (43 [36-50] versus 48 [41-56]). Core service mismatch, defined by high aging and low output, was concentrated in county-and-below hospitals, which accounted for 70.9% of the total area. Aging rate was associated with achieving a median DNT of ≤60 min (absolute probability difference (%), 2.85; 95% confidence interval, 0.97-4.73; p = 0.003, per 10% increase). Exploratory analysis suggested that larger aging populations were associated with greater thrombolysis volume, which was, in turn, associated with shorter DNT. Geographic disparities and service output mismatch persisted within China's AIS care network. Given the dual associations between population aging and reperfusion therapy service, capacity building in basic hospitals and demographic-based resource allocation may help align services with regional needs. This work was supported by the Beijing Natural Science Foundation.

title: Brainstem orexigenic neurons drive long-term energy balance via distributed hypothalamic circuits.
abstract: Energy balance control has long been primarily attributed to hypothalamic neurons, whereas the physiological contribution of brainstem feeding circuits to sustained long-term hyperphagia and weight gain remains poorly defined. Here, we combined viral tracing, optogenetics, chronic chemogenetics, and targeted neuronal ablation to functionally characterize the brainstem neuropeptide Y (NPY) neuronal circuit and define its critical roles in regulating feeding behavior and long-term body weight homeostasis. NPY neurons in the nucleus of solitary tract (NTSNPY) send parallel, partially overlapping excitatory collaterals to the hypothalamus, each independently driving feeding. Their orexigenic effects persist following the ablation of hypothalamic AgRP/NPY neurons. Chronic NTSNPY activation induces persistent hyperphagia and weight gain, whereas single or dual ablation of NTSNPY plus hypothalamic AgRP/NPY failed to disrupt baseline energy homeostasis, revealing redundant brain orexigenic networks. Our data identify NTSNPY neurons as an extra-hypothalamic pro-obesogenic population independent of canonical AgRP circuits, offering a therapeutic target for obesity.

title: Discrete functional regions of the olfactory bulb represent region-specific molecular feature sets.
abstract: In the mammalian brain, odors are encoded by combinatorial activation of the glomeruli in the olfactory bulb. The topography of the bulb has been described as tunotopic or chemotopic, such that glomeruli with similar odor tuning or similar chemical property tuning are spatially close. However, several aspects of the bulb topography remain debated, in particular whether there are discrete regions of glomeruli with similar odor tuning, as opposed to a continuous tunotopic mapping, and whether commonly used molecular features have predictive power for the odor responses and are mapped to specific regions. Here, we measured glomerular odor responses in the mouse olfactory bulb by calcium imaging and analyzed the map between (1) the functional space of glomerular odor responses, (2) the two-dimensional bulb surface, and (3) the chemical space of molecular features. We found an organization of the bulb surface into discrete functional regions consisting of glomeruli with similar odor tuning and with functional discontinuities at the region boundaries. The glomeruli within the same functional region also had similar temporal response dynamics, independent of response amplitude. The chemical property tuning of the regions could be described by region-specific molecular feature sets with region-specific predictive power for the odor responses. Our results suggest a fragmented tuno- and chemotopic organization of the bulb, where glomeruli within the same functional region are tuned to similar chemical properties and are temporally synchronized, which is potentially beneficial for local signal processing.

title: Egg-ception to the rule: Monocyte-derived microglia infiltrate CVOs.
abstract: Circumventricular organs (CVOs) are specialized interfaces between the peripheral circulation and the brain. In this issue of Immunity, Van Hove et al. reveal CVOs as distinct immune niches that shape brain macrophage identity. These environments generate specialized macrophage phenotypes and enable fetal monocytes to adopt bona fide microglial identities, thereby demonstrating how local tissue context can influence immune cell fate.

title: Pyruvate dehydrogenase inhibition suppresses paclitaxel-induced nociceptive hypersensitivity in Drosophila and mice.
abstract: Paclitaxel is widely used against solid tumors, but painful sensory neuropathy frequently limits its dosing, and no therapy has been approved to prevent or reverse this complication. Mitochondrial injury in sensory neurons is increasingly recognized as a contributor to paclitaxel-induced peripheral neuropathy (PIPN), although the metabolic sources of this injury remain poorly defined. We therefore asked whether blocking the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex (PDH), which releases hydrogen peroxide as a byproduct of acetyl-CoA synthesis, could prevent PIPN. In fruit fly larvae, dietary paclitaxel caused heat hypersensitivity together with excessive dendrite growth and branching in class IV dendritic arborization (C4da) nociceptors, and a small-molecule PDH inhibitor reversed these changes. The inhibitor also blocked the paclitaxel-driven rise in mitochondrial ROS and mitophagy within C4da neurons. Lowering PDH activity genetically, through knockdown of the PDH E1α subunit, mutation of the PDH phosphatase, or overexpression of PDH kinase, likewise protected larvae from paclitaxel-induced thermal hyperalgesia. In mice, systemic PDH inhibition attenuated mechanical allodynia caused by repeated paclitaxel injections. These findings indicate that PDH activity contributes to paclitaxel-induced sensory hypersensitivity, suggest that mitochondrial oxidative stress may be involved, and support PDH inhibition as a potential preventive strategy against chemotherapy-induced neuropathy.

title: Preparation of wood-derived cellulose sheets with anisotropic topology and surface carboxylation and investigation of their cell-material interactions.
abstract: Surface micropatterns featuring unique anisotropic topological architectures are essential for regulating cellular behaviors. In this work, natural balsa wood was employed as a template. Through conventional delignification combined with in-situ carboxylation modification using hydrated deep eutectic solvent, followed by water plasticization swelling and mechanical exfoliation, cellulose sheets integrating intrinsic topological features and surface chemical activity were successfully fabricated. L929 fibroblasts and C17.2 neural stem cells were subsequently adopted as cell models to investigate cell-material interactions. Physicochemical characterizations demonstrated that the sheets possessed a high carboxylation content of 1.44 mmol/g while completely retaining the multiscale anisotropic topological morphology of native wood. In vitro biological assessments validated the as-prepared sheets' excellent biocompatibility. Finally, this study shows that the intrinsic anisotropic microgroove topography of cellulose sheets provides the physical structure for cell orientation, while surface carboxylation further enhances cell alignment along these microgrooves. This research provides a feasible strategy for constructing multiscale bioactive scaffolds derived from natural wood, which holds promising application prospects for the repair and regeneration of intricate anisotropic tissues.

title: Lysosome-targeted near-infrared fluorescent probe ROCL enables dynamic hypochlorous acid imaging in living cells and a mouse model of Parkinson's disease.
journal: Spectrochimica acta. Part A, Molecular and biomolecular spectroscopy
abstract: Hypochlorous acid (HClO) plays critical roles in oxidative stress and is strongly implicated in the progression of Parkinson's disease (PD). Here, we report ROCL, a new lysosome-targeted near-infrared fluorescent probe for sensitive and selective detection of HClO in living systems. ROCL displays rapid response, excellent selectivity, and a low detection limit of 49 nM, based on an HClO-induced spirolactam ring-opening mechanism. The probe enables real-time imaging of exogenous and endogenous HClO in SH-SY5Y and PC12 cells, exhibits low cytotoxicity, and effectively visualizes elevated HClO levels in MPTP- and rotenone-induced PD models. ROCL also shows favorable blood-brain barrier permeability and allows noninvasive in vivo HClO imaging in PD model mice. These results establish ROCL as a valuable tool for probing HClO-associated oxidative stress in neurodegenerative diseases.

title: Combining transcranial electrical and magnetic stimulation: a scoping review of neurophysiological and clinical studies.
journal: Clinical neurophysiology : official journal of the International Federation of Clinical Neurophysiology
abstract: Clinical response to repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) and transcranial electrical stimulation (tES) is variable. Combining these techniques may improve effectiveness. The aim of this review is to map how rTMS and tES have been combined so far in both neurophysiological and clinical studies. Three databases were searched: Embase, MEDLINE, and APA PsychInfo. Included articles compared a combination of rTMS and tES, against a single form of stimulation (either rTMS or tES). Sixty-seven articles were included. Forty studies examined the impact of combined stimulation on a measure of neurophysiology in healthy volunteers. Most studies targeted the motor cortex (25) and used transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) (25) combined with a form of rTMS, either applying stimulation simultaneously (19) or with tES priming of rTMS (14). Twenty-seven studies used combined stimulation to treat people with a health condition (including people with tinnitus, depression, bipolar, Parkinson's disease, and post-stroke motor deficits). Studies indicate that tES could enhance or reverse expected effects of rTMS. The greatest increase in cortical excitability occurred following excitatory rTMS combined with gamma transcranial alternating current stimulation (tACS) or with cathodal tDCS, consistent with effects of metaplasticity. Cathodal tDCS combined with excitatory rTMS has shown promise for treating depression and post-stroke motor deficits. This review highlights combined stimulation as a promising method to modulate and enhance the neurophysiological and clinical effects of rTMS and tES. Insights from neurophysiological studies may guide development of more effective clinical treatments.
